segment.text: Divergences from the grammar described here occur in some historical, social, cultural, and regional varieties of English, although these are minor compared to the differences in pronunciation and vocabulary .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2846-3056", "next_segment_id": "lseg-9d4d3bd7abde", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-0fd0076ca715", "segment_id": "lseg-621211f60fbb", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Divergences from the grammar described here occur in some historical, social, cultural, and regional varieties of English, although these are minor compared to the differences in pronunciation and vocabulary ."}}

segment.text: Modern English has largely abandoned the inflectional case system of Indo-European in favor of analytic constructions.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3056-3175", "next_segment_id": "lseg-5408665500e6", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-621211f60fbb", "segment_id": "lseg-9d4d3bd7abde", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Modern English has largely abandoned the inflectional case system of Indo-European in favor of analytic constructions."}}

segment.text: The personal pronouns retain morphological case more strongly than any other word class (a remnant of the more extensive Germanic case system of Old English).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3175-3334", "next_segment_id": "lseg-1153f93343bd", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-9d4d3bd7abde", "segment_id": "lseg-5408665500e6", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The personal pronouns retain morphological case more strongly than any other word class (a remnant of the more extensive Germanic case system of Old English)."}}

segment.text: For other pronouns, and all nouns, adjectives, and articles, grammatical function is indicated only by word order , by prepositions , and by the " Saxon genitive or English possessive " ( -'s ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3334-3529", "next_segment_id": "lseg-85672701e4b9", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-5408665500e6", "segment_id": "lseg-1153f93343bd", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "For other pronouns, and all nouns, adjectives, and articles, grammatical function is indicated only by word order , by prepositions , and by the \" Saxon genitive or English possessive \" ( -'s )."}}

segment.text: [ 2 ] The rest are closed classes ; for example, it is rare for a new pronoun to enter the language.

segment.text: Determiners, traditionally classified along with adjectives, have not always been regarded as a separate part of speech.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:4691-4812", "next_segment_id": "lseg-1f4917627d20", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-a4acfa56958a", "segment_id": "lseg-36586fa49a2f", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Determiners, traditionally classified along with adjectives, have not always been regarded as a separate part of speech."}}

segment.text: Interjections are another word class, but these are not described here as they do not form part of the clause and sentence structure of the language.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:4812-4962", "next_segment_id": "lseg-d7d0730fb63a", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-36586fa49a2f", "segment_id": "lseg-1f4917627d20", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Interjections are another word class, but these are not described here as they do not form part of the clause and sentence structure of the language."}}

segment.text: [ 2 ] Linguists generally accept nine English word classes: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions, determiners, and exclamations.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:4962-5126", "next_segment_id": "lseg-2978aebf8a6e", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-1f4917627d20", "segment_id": "lseg-d7d0730fb63a", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 2 ] Linguists generally accept nine English word classes: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions, determiners, and exclamations."}}

segment.text: English words are not generally marked for word class.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5126-5181", "next_segment_id": "lseg-638f07588f72", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-d7d0730fb63a", "segment_id": "lseg-2978aebf8a6e", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "English words are not generally marked for word class."}}

segment.text: It is not usually possible to tell from the form of a word which class it belongs to, but some inflectional endings and derivational suffixes are distinct to each class.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5181-5351", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b0fe20e017f3", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-2978aebf8a6e", "segment_id": "lseg-638f07588f72", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "It is not usually possible to tell from the form of a word which class it belongs to, but some inflectional endings and derivational suffixes are distinct to each class."}}

segment.text: On the other hand, most words belong to more than one word class.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5351-5417", "next_segment_id": "lseg-833a17e7d1c9", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-638f07588f72", "segment_id": "lseg-b0fe20e017f3", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "On the other hand, most words belong to more than one word class."}}

segment.text: For example, run can serve as either a verb or a noun (these are regarded as two different lexemes ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5417-5519", "next_segment_id": "lseg-07deb2b901d9", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-b0fe20e017f3", "segment_id": "lseg-833a17e7d1c9", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "For example, run can serve as either a verb or a noun (these are regarded as two different lexemes )."}}

segment.text: [ 3 ] Lexemes may be inflected to express different grammatical categories.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5519-5595", "next_segment_id": "lseg-1d78b6d3e055", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-833a17e7d1c9", "segment_id": "lseg-07deb2b901d9", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 3 ] Lexemes may be inflected to express different grammatical categories."}}

segment.text: The lexeme run has the forms runs , ran , runny , runner , and running .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5595-5668", "next_segment_id": "lseg-6ae5af22ae6b", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-07deb2b901d9", "segment_id": "lseg-1d78b6d3e055", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The lexeme run has the forms runs , ran , runny , runner , and running ."}}

segment.text: [ 3 ] Words in one class can sometimes be derived from those in another.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5668-5741", "next_segment_id": "lseg-5a18a5a3755f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-1d78b6d3e055", "segment_id": "lseg-6ae5af22ae6b", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 3 ] Words in one class can sometimes be derived from those in another."}}

segment.text: This has the potential to give rise to new words.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5741-5791", "next_segment_id": "lseg-1bc85bc56f5f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-6ae5af22ae6b", "segment_id": "lseg-5a18a5a3755f", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "This has the potential to give rise to new words."}}

segment.text: For example, the noun aerobics has given rise to the adjective aerobicized .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5791-5868", "next_segment_id": "lseg-c82122d21491", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-5a18a5a3755f", "segment_id": "lseg-1bc85bc56f5f", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "For example, the noun aerobics has given rise to the adjective aerobicized ."}}

language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5868-5906", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b9a78c639eff", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-1bc85bc56f5f", "segment_id": "lseg-c82122d21491", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 3 ] Words combine to form phrases ."}}

segment.text: A phrase typically serves the same function as a word from some particular word class.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5906-5993", "next_segment_id": "lseg-4acf48b8644d", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-c82122d21491", "segment_id": "lseg-b9a78c639eff", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "A phrase typically serves the same function as a word from some particular word class."}}

segment.text: [ 3 ] For example, my very good friend Peter is a phrase that can be used in a sentence as if it were a noun, and is therefore called a noun phrase .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5993-6143", "next_segment_id": "lseg-9805fa9765c4", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-b9a78c639eff", "segment_id": "lseg-4acf48b8644d", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 3 ] For example, my very good friend Peter is a phrase that can be used in a sentence as if it were a noun, and is therefore called a noun phrase ."}}

segment.text: Similarly, adjectival phrases and adverbial phrases function as if they were adjectives or adverbs, but with other types of phrases, the terminology has different implications.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:6143-6320", "next_segment_id": "lseg-bdcfdcd27ac9", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-4acf48b8644d", "segment_id": "lseg-9805fa9765c4", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Similarly, adjectival phrases and adverbial phrases function as if they were adjectives or adverbs, but with other types of phrases, the terminology has different implications."}}

segment.text: For example, a verb phrase consists of a verb together with any objects and other dependents; a prepositional phrase consists of a preposition and its complement (and is therefore usually a type of adverbial phrase); and a determiner phrase is a type of noun phrase containing a determiner.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:6320-6611", "next_segment_id": "lseg-e25bb93b7b66", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-9805fa9765c4", "segment_id": "lseg-bdcfdcd27ac9", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "For example, a verb phrase consists of a verb together with any objects and other dependents; a prepositional phrase consists of a preposition and its complement (and is therefore usually a type of adverbial phrase); and a determiner phrase is a type of noun phrase containing a determiner."}}

segment.text: Nouns [ edit ] Main article: English nouns Many common suffixes form nouns from other nouns or from other types of words, such as -age ( shrinkage ), -hood ( sisterhood ), and so on, [ 3 ] though many nouns are base forms containing no such suffix ( cat , grass , France ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:6611-6885", "next_segment_id": "lseg-89a966230b87", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-bdcfdcd27ac9", "segment_id": "lseg-e25bb93b7b66", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Nouns [ edit ] Main article: English nouns Many common suffixes form nouns from other nouns or from other types of words, such as -age ( shrinkage ), -hood ( sisterhood ), and so on, [ 3 ] though many nouns are base forms containing no such suffix ( cat , grass , France )."}}

segment.text: Nouns are also created by converting verbs and adjectives, as with the words talk and reading ( a boring talk , the assigned reading ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:6885-7021", "next_segment_id": "lseg-54d51331bb52", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-e25bb93b7b66", "segment_id": "lseg-89a966230b87", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Nouns are also created by converting verbs and adjectives, as with the words talk and reading ( a boring talk , the assigned reading )."}}

segment.text: Nouns are sometimes classified semantically (by their meanings) as proper and common nouns ( Cyrus , China vs frog , milk ) or as concrete and abstract nouns ( book , laptop vs embarrassment , prejudice ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:7021-7227", "next_segment_id": "lseg-e085b225d964", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-89a966230b87", "segment_id": "lseg-54d51331bb52", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Nouns are sometimes classified semantically (by their meanings) as proper and common nouns ( Cyrus , China vs frog , milk ) or as concrete and abstract nouns ( book , laptop vs embarrassment , prejudice )."}}

segment.text: [ 4 ] A grammatical distinction is often made between count (countable) nouns such as clock and city , and non-count (uncountable) nouns such as milk and decor .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:7227-7389", "next_segment_id": "lseg-be081be8f9ea", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-54d51331bb52", "segment_id": "lseg-e085b225d964", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 4 ] A grammatical distinction is often made between count (countable) nouns such as clock and city , and non-count (uncountable) nouns such as milk and decor ."}}

segment.text: [ 5 ] Some nouns can function both as countable and as uncountable such as "wine" in This is a good wine .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:7389-7496", "next_segment_id": "lseg-035753eeb59b", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-e085b225d964", "segment_id": "lseg-be081be8f9ea", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 5 ] Some nouns can function both as countable and as uncountable such as \"wine\" in This is a good wine ."}}

segment.text: Countable nouns generally have singular and plural forms.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:7496-7554", "next_segment_id": "lseg-924761108143", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-be081be8f9ea", "segment_id": "lseg-035753eeb59b", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Countable nouns generally have singular and plural forms."}}

segment.text: [ 4 ] In most cases the plural is formed from the singular by adding -[e]s (as in dogs , bushes ), although there are also irregular forms ( woman/women , foot/feet ), including cases where the two forms are identical ( sheep , series ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:7554-7792", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b14cb176bedc", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-035753eeb59b", "segment_id": "lseg-924761108143", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 4 ] In most cases the plural is formed from the singular by adding -[e]s (as in dogs , bushes ), although there are also irregular forms ( woman/women , foot/feet ), including cases where the two forms are identical ( sheep , series )."}}

segment.text: For more details see English plural .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:7792-7830", "next_segment_id": "lseg-95c75801b885", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-924761108143", "segment_id": "lseg-b14cb176bedc", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "For more details see English plural ."}}

segment.text: Certain nouns can be used with plural verbs even though they are singular in form, as in The government were .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:7830-7941", "next_segment_id": "lseg-71be38461076", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-b14cb176bedc", "segment_id": "lseg-95c75801b885", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Certain nouns can be used with plural verbs even though they are singular in form, as in The government were ."}}

segment.text: (where the government is considered to refer to the people constituting the government).

segment.text: English nouns are not marked for case as they are in some languages, but they have possessive forms, through the addition of -'s (as in John's , children's ) or just an apostrophe (with no change in pronunciation) in the case of -[e]s plurals ( the dogs' owners ) and sometimes other words ending with -s ( Jesus' love ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:8188-8510", "next_segment_id": "lseg-88195aabb312", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-67bc7189a0a1", "segment_id": "lseg-8978de9d550f", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "English nouns are not marked for case as they are in some languages, but they have possessive forms, through the addition of -'s (as in John's , children's ) or just an apostrophe (with no change in pronunciation) in the case of -[e]s plurals ( the dogs' owners ) and sometimes other words ending with -s ( Jesus' love )."}}

segment.text: More generally the ending can be applied to noun phrases (as in the man you saw yesterday's sister ); see below.

segment.text: The third-person singular forms are differentiated according to the gender of the referent.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:18618-18710", "next_segment_id": "lseg-7411b639023a", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-1078aad7e170", "segment_id": "lseg-676cc5b45829", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The third-person singular forms are differentiated according to the gender of the referent."}}

segment.text: For example, she is used to refer to a woman, sometimes a female animal, and sometimes an object to which feminine characteristics are attributed, such as a ship or a country.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:18710-18886", "next_segment_id": "lseg-899416be8206", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-676cc5b45829", "segment_id": "lseg-7411b639023a", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "For example, she is used to refer to a woman, sometimes a female animal, and sometimes an object to which feminine characteristics are attributed, such as a ship or a country."}}

segment.text: A man, and sometimes a male animal, is referred to using he .

segment.text: Historically, singular they was restricted to quantificational constructions such as Each employee should clean their desk and referential cases where the referent's gender was unknown.

segment.text: However, it is increasingly used when the referent's gender is irrelevant or when the referent is neither male nor female.

segment.text: The possessive determiners such as my are used as determiners together with nouns, as in my old man , some of his friends .

segment.text: The second possessive forms like mine are used when they do not qualify a noun: as pronouns, as in mine is bigger than yours , and as predicates, as in this one is mine .

segment.text: Demonstrative [ edit ] The demonstrative pronouns of English are this (plural these ), and that (plural those ), as in these are good, I like that .

segment.text: All four words can also be used as determiners (followed by a noun), as in those cars .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:20105-20193", "next_segment_id": "lseg-7f2f6e52b4de", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-387345d20c7a", "segment_id": "lseg-141da073f502", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "All four words can also be used as determiners (followed by a noun), as in those cars ."}}

segment.text: They can also form the alternative pronominal expressions this/that one , these/those ones .

segment.text: Interrogative [ edit ] The interrogative pronouns are who , what , and which (all of them can take the suffix -ever for emphasis).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:20286-20417", "next_segment_id": "lseg-56db00215bcd", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-7f2f6e52b4de", "segment_id": "lseg-6a9065a1d00a", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Interrogative [ edit ] The interrogative pronouns are who , what , and which (all of them can take the suffix -ever for emphasis)."}}

segment.text: The pronoun who refers to a person or people; it has an oblique form whom (though in informal contexts this is usually replaced by who ), and a possessive form (pronoun or determiner) whose .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:20417-20609", "next_segment_id": "lseg-a11ced0c299f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-6a9065a1d00a", "segment_id": "lseg-56db00215bcd", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The pronoun who refers to a person or people; it has an oblique form whom (though in informal contexts this is usually replaced by who ), and a possessive form (pronoun or determiner) whose ."}}

segment.text: The pronoun what refers to things or abstracts.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:20609-20657", "next_segment_id": "lseg-22c63bc232f7", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-56db00215bcd", "segment_id": "lseg-a11ced0c299f", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The pronoun what refers to things or abstracts."}}

segment.text: The word which is used to ask about alternatives from what is seen as a closed set: which (of the books) do you like best?

segment.text: In Old and Middle English, the roles of the three words were different from their roles today.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:21092-21187", "next_segment_id": "lseg-d7262e4a12a6", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-6591ad95ca39", "segment_id": "lseg-3eebbbeabe12", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "In Old and Middle English, the roles of the three words were different from their roles today."}}

segment.text: "The interrogative pronoun hwā 'who, what' had only singular forms and also only distinguished between non-neuter and neuter, the neuter nominative form being hwæt ".

segment.text: [ 15 ] Note that neuter and non-neuter refers to the grammatical gender system of the time, rather than the so-called natural gender system of today.

segment.text: The main relative pronouns in English are who (with its derived forms whom and whose ), which , and that .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:21906-22013", "next_segment_id": "lseg-ef07e8bf61f3", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-3fdd739b47de", "segment_id": "lseg-a009c45416f4", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The main relative pronouns in English are who (with its derived forms whom and whose ), which , and that ."}}

segment.text: [ 16 ] The relative pronoun which refers to things rather than persons, as in the shirt, which used to be red, is faded .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:22013-22135", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b48737f31019", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-a009c45416f4", "segment_id": "lseg-ef07e8bf61f3", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 16 ] The relative pronoun which refers to things rather than persons, as in the shirt, which used to be red, is faded ."}}

segment.text: For persons, who is used ( the man who saw me was tall ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:22135-22193", "next_segment_id": "lseg-9c8725e0df1b", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-ef07e8bf61f3", "segment_id": "lseg-b48737f31019", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "For persons, who is used ( the man who saw me was tall )."}}

segment.text: The oblique case form of who is whom , as in the man whom I saw was tall , although in informal registers who is commonly used in place of whom .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:22193-22339", "next_segment_id": "lseg-9474464dcb30", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-b48737f31019", "segment_id": "lseg-9c8725e0df1b", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The oblique case form of who is whom , as in the man whom I saw was tall , although in informal registers who is commonly used in place of whom ."}}

segment.text: The possessive form of who is whose (for example, the man whose car is missing ); however the use of whose is not restricted to persons (one can say an idea whose time has come ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:22339-22519", "next_segment_id": "lseg-287994a76b11", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-9c8725e0df1b", "segment_id": "lseg-9474464dcb30", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The possessive form of who is whose (for example, the man whose car is missing ); however the use of whose is not restricted to persons (one can say an idea whose time has come )."}}

segment.text: The word that as a relative pronoun is normally found only in restrictive relative clauses (unlike which and who , which can be used in both restrictive and unrestrictive clauses).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:22519-22700", "next_segment_id": "lseg-1291024b5064", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-9474464dcb30", "segment_id": "lseg-287994a76b11", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The word that as a relative pronoun is normally found only in restrictive relative clauses (unlike which and who , which can be used in both restrictive and unrestrictive clauses)."}}

segment.text: It can refer to either persons or things, and cannot follow a preposition.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:22700-22775", "next_segment_id": "lseg-331b4cd074ec", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-287994a76b11", "segment_id": "lseg-1291024b5064", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "It can refer to either persons or things, and cannot follow a preposition."}}

segment.text: For example, one can say the song that [or which ] I listened to yesterday , but the song to which [not to that ] I listened yesterday .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:22775-22912", "next_segment_id": "lseg-ef91869cf907", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-1291024b5064", "segment_id": "lseg-331b4cd074ec", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "For example, one can say the song that [or which ] I listened to yesterday , but the song to which [not to that ] I listened yesterday ."}}

segment.text: The relative pronoun that is usually pronounced with a reduced vowel ( schwa ), and hence differently from the demonstrative that (see Weak and strong forms in English ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:22912-23083", "next_segment_id": "lseg-9e01c9638c76", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-331b4cd074ec", "segment_id": "lseg-ef91869cf907", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The relative pronoun that is usually pronounced with a reduced vowel ( schwa ), and hence differently from the demonstrative that (see Weak and strong forms in English )."}}

segment.text: If that is not the subject of the relative clause, it can be omitted ( the song I listened to yesterday ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:23083-23190", "next_segment_id": "lseg-bac04ec90456", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-ef91869cf907", "segment_id": "lseg-9e01c9638c76", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "If that is not the subject of the relative clause, it can be omitted ( the song I listened to yesterday )."}}

segment.text: The word what can be used to form a free relative clause – one that has no antecedent and that serves as a complete noun phrase in itself, as in I like what he likes .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:23190-23358", "next_segment_id": "lseg-d2b0543aad44", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-9e01c9638c76", "segment_id": "lseg-bac04ec90456", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The word what can be used to form a free relative clause – one that has no antecedent and that serves as a complete noun phrase in itself, as in I like what he likes ."}}

segment.text: The words whatever and whichever can be used similarly, in the role of either pronouns ( whatever he likes ) or determiners ( whatever book he likes ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:23358-23510", "next_segment_id": "lseg-0c24aee5a665", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-bac04ec90456", "segment_id": "lseg-d2b0543aad44", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The words whatever and whichever can be used similarly, in the role of either pronouns ( whatever he likes ) or determiners ( whatever book he likes )."}}

segment.text: When referring to persons, who(ever) (and whom(ever) ) can be used in a similar way.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:23510-23595", "next_segment_id": "lseg-03854215db57", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-d2b0543aad44", "segment_id": "lseg-0c24aee5a665", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "When referring to persons, who(ever) (and whom(ever) ) can be used in a similar way."}}

segment.text: "There" [ edit ] The word there is used as a pronoun in some sentences, playing the role of a dummy subject , normally of an intransitive verb .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:23595-23740", "next_segment_id": "lseg-4c9cab895ef4", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-0c24aee5a665", "segment_id": "lseg-03854215db57", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "\"There\" [ edit ] The word there is used as a pronoun in some sentences, playing the role of a dummy subject , normally of an intransitive verb ."}}

segment.text: The "logical subject" of the verb then appears as a complement after the verb.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:23740-23819", "next_segment_id": "lseg-06dcf201c907", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-03854215db57", "segment_id": "lseg-4c9cab895ef4", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The \"logical subject\" of the verb then appears as a complement after the verb."}}

segment.text: This use of there occurs most commonly with forms of the verb be in existential clauses , to refer to the presence or existence of something.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:23819-23961", "next_segment_id": "lseg-718102612847", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-4c9cab895ef4", "segment_id": "lseg-06dcf201c907", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "This use of there occurs most commonly with forms of the verb be in existential clauses , to refer to the presence or existence of something."}}

segment.text: For example: There is a heaven ; There are two cups on the table ; There have been a lot of problems lately .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:23961-24071", "next_segment_id": "lseg-857713f7e847", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-06dcf201c907", "segment_id": "lseg-718102612847", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "For example: There is a heaven ; There are two cups on the table ; There have been a lot of problems lately ."}}

segment.text: It can also be used with other verbs: There exist two major variants ; There occurred a very strange incident .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:24071-24183", "next_segment_id": "lseg-2e69f0372ee8", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-718102612847", "segment_id": "lseg-857713f7e847", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "It can also be used with other verbs: There exist two major variants ; There occurred a very strange incident ."}}

segment.text: The dummy subject takes the number (singular or plural) of the logical subject (complement), hence it takes a plural verb if the complement is plural.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:24183-24334", "next_segment_id": "lseg-a19505d2ce1f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-857713f7e847", "segment_id": "lseg-2e69f0372ee8", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The dummy subject takes the number (singular or plural) of the logical subject (complement), hence it takes a plural verb if the complement is plural."}}

segment.text: In informal English, however, the contraction there's is often used for both singular and plural.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:24334-24432", "next_segment_id": "lseg-aa8a77e3621c", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-2e69f0372ee8", "segment_id": "lseg-a19505d2ce1f", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "In informal English, however, the contraction there's is often used for both singular and plural."}}

segment.text: [ 17 ] The dummy subject can undergo inversion , Is there a test today?

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:24432-24504", "next_segment_id": "lseg-2bd1b1881a73", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-a19505d2ce1f", "segment_id": "lseg-aa8a77e3621c", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 17 ] The dummy subject can undergo inversion , Is there a test today?"}}

segment.text: The word there in such sentences has sometimes been analyzed as an adverb , or as a dummy predicate , rather than as a pronoun.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:24699-24827", "next_segment_id": "lseg-814cccccbd84", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-62dcb177bc6c", "segment_id": "lseg-af3f70b54a87", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The word there in such sentences has sometimes been analyzed as an adverb , or as a dummy predicate , rather than as a pronoun."}}

segment.text: [ 18 ] However, its identification as a pronoun is most consistent with its behavior in inverted sentences and question tags as described above.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:24827-24972", "next_segment_id": "lseg-31d594801e9e", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-af3f70b54a87", "segment_id": "lseg-814cccccbd84", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 18 ] However, its identification as a pronoun is most consistent with its behavior in inverted sentences and question tags as described above."}}

segment.text: Because the word there can also be a deictic adverb (meaning "at/to that place"), a sentence like There is a river could have either of two meanings: "a river exists" (with there as a pronoun), and "a river is in that place" (with there as an adverb).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:24972-25224", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b4e48dce290a", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-814cccccbd84", "segment_id": "lseg-31d594801e9e", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Because the word there can also be a deictic adverb (meaning \"at/to that place\"), a sentence like There is a river could have either of two meanings: \"a river exists\" (with there as a pronoun), and \"a river is in that place\" (with there as an adverb)."}}

segment.text: In speech, the adverbial there would be given stress , while the pronoun would not – in fact, the pronoun is often pronounced as a weak form , /ðə(r)/ .

segment.text: Reciprocal [ edit ] The English reciprocal pronouns are each other and one another .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:25377-25462", "next_segment_id": "lseg-aeaeea835be2", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-b4e48dce290a", "segment_id": "lseg-482b003392fe", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Reciprocal [ edit ] The English reciprocal pronouns are each other and one another ."}}

segment.text: No consistent distinction in meaning or use can be found between them.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:25462-25533", "next_segment_id": "lseg-4fc486117b8c", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-482b003392fe", "segment_id": "lseg-aeaeea835be2", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "No consistent distinction in meaning or use can be found between them."}}

segment.text: Like the reflexive pronouns, their use is limited to contexts where an antecedent precedes it.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:25533-25628", "next_segment_id": "lseg-56b20b2bae5d", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-aeaeea835be2", "segment_id": "lseg-4fc486117b8c", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Like the reflexive pronouns, their use is limited to contexts where an antecedent precedes it."}}

segment.text: In the case of the reciprocals, they need to appear in the same clause as the antecedent.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:25628-25718", "next_segment_id": "lseg-2c043ecccd83", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-4fc486117b8c", "segment_id": "lseg-56b20b2bae5d", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "In the case of the reciprocals, they need to appear in the same clause as the antecedent."}}

segment.text: [ 1 ] Other [ edit ] Other pronouns in English are often identical in form to determiners (especially quantifiers ), such as many , a little , etc.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:25718-25866", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b77d75958979", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-56b20b2bae5d", "segment_id": "lseg-2c043ecccd83", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 1 ] Other [ edit ] Other pronouns in English are often identical in form to determiners (especially quantifiers ), such as many , a little , etc."}}

segment.text: Sometimes, the pronoun form is different, as with none (corresponding to the determiner no ), nothing , everyone , somebody , etc.

segment.text: [ 19 ] Verbs [ edit ] Main article: English verbs The basic form of an English verb is not generally marked by any ending, although there are certain suffixes that are frequently used to form verbs, such as -ate ( formulate ), -fy ( electrify ), and -ise/ize ( realise/realize ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:26206-26486", "next_segment_id": "lseg-6fe6562c7cfb", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-2efdbbffbdec", "segment_id": "lseg-a151728f5af9", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 19 ] Verbs [ edit ] Main article: English verbs The basic form of an English verb is not generally marked by any ending, although there are certain suffixes that are frequently used to form verbs, such as -ate ( formulate ), -fy ( electrify ), and -ise/ize ( realise/realize )."}}

segment.text: [ 20 ] Many verbs also contain prefixes , such as un- ( unmask ), out- ( outlast ), over- ( overtake ), and under- ( undervalue ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:26486-26617", "next_segment_id": "lseg-6d0d7825efe7", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-a151728f5af9", "segment_id": "lseg-6fe6562c7cfb", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 20 ] Many verbs also contain prefixes , such as un- ( unmask ), out- ( outlast ), over- ( overtake ), and under- ( undervalue )."}}

segment.text: [ 20 ] Verbs can also be formed from nouns and adjectives by zero derivation , as with the verbs snare , nose , dry , and calm .

segment.text: Most verbs have three or four inflected forms in addition to the base form: a third-person singular present tense form in -(e)s ( writes , botches ), a present participle and gerund form in -ing ( writing ), a past tense ( wrote ), and – though often identical to the past tense form – a past participle ( written ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:26746-27063", "next_segment_id": "lseg-db6cf97d1b78", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-6d0d7825efe7", "segment_id": "lseg-4f20ec79b82a", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Most verbs have three or four inflected forms in addition to the base form: a third-person singular present tense form in -(e)s ( writes , botches ), a present participle and gerund form in -ing ( writing ), a past tense ( wrote ), and – though often identical to the past tense form – a past participle ( written )."}}

segment.text: Regular verbs have identical past tense and past participle forms in -ed , but there are 100 or so irregular English verbs with different forms (see list ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:27063-27220", "next_segment_id": "lseg-587ce7fb5ecf", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-4f20ec79b82a", "segment_id": "lseg-db6cf97d1b78", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Regular verbs have identical past tense and past participle forms in -ed , but there are 100 or so irregular English verbs with different forms (see list )."}}

segment.text: The verbs have , do and say also have irregular third-person present tense forms ( has , does /dʌz/ , says /sɛz/ ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:27220-27336", "next_segment_id": "lseg-9e7fb336e7e7", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-db6cf97d1b78", "segment_id": "lseg-587ce7fb5ecf", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The verbs have , do and say also have irregular third-person present tense forms ( has , does /dʌz/ , says /sɛz/ )."}}

segment.text: The verb be has the largest number of irregular forms ( am, is, are in the present tense, was, were in the past tense, been for the past participle).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:27336-27486", "next_segment_id": "lseg-d994c7e05d65", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-587ce7fb5ecf", "segment_id": "lseg-9e7fb336e7e7", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The verb be has the largest number of irregular forms ( am, is, are in the present tense, was, were in the past tense, been for the past participle)."}}

segment.text: Most of what are often referred to as verb tenses (or sometimes aspects ) in English are formed using auxiliary verbs .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:27486-27606", "next_segment_id": "lseg-1748230c74eb", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-9e7fb336e7e7", "segment_id": "lseg-d994c7e05d65", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Most of what are often referred to as verb tenses (or sometimes aspects ) in English are formed using auxiliary verbs ."}}

segment.text: Apart from what are called the simple present ( write , writes ) and simple past ( wrote ), there are also continuous (progressive) forms ( am/is/are/was/were writing ), perfect forms ( have/has/had written , and the perfect continuous have/has/had been writing ), future forms ( will write , will be writing , will have written , will have been writing ), and conditionals (also called " future in the past "), so forms equivalent to future ones but with would instead of will .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:27606-28086", "next_segment_id": "lseg-e5f3a99ee8a5", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-d994c7e05d65", "segment_id": "lseg-1748230c74eb", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Apart from what are called the simple present ( write , writes ) and simple past ( wrote ), there are also continuous (progressive) forms ( am/is/are/was/were writing ), perfect forms ( have/has/had written , and the perfect continuous have/has/had been writing ), future forms ( will write , will be writing , will have written , will have been writing ), and conditionals (also called \" future in the past \"), so forms equivalent to future ones but with would instead of will ."}}

segment.text: The auxiliaries shall and should sometimes replace will and would in the first person.

segment.text: Phrases [ edit ] A verb together with its dependents, excluding its subject , may be identified as a verb phrase (although this concept is not acknowledged in all theories of grammar [ 24 ] ).

segment.text: A verb phrase headed by a finite verb may also be called a predicate .

segment.text: The dependents may be objects , complements, and modifiers (adverbs or adverbial phrases ).

segment.text: In English, objects and complements nearly always come after the verb; a direct object precedes other complements such as prepositional phrases, but if there is an indirect object as well, expressed without a preposition, then that precedes the direct object: give me the book , but give the book to me .

segment.text: Adverbial modifiers generally follow objects, although other positions are possible (see under § Adverbs below).

segment.text: Adjectives [ edit ] Main article: English adjectives English adjectives , as with other word classes, cannot in general be identified as such by their form, [ 25 ] although many of them are formed from nouns or other words by the addition of a suffix, such as -al ( habitual ), -ful ( blissful ), -ic ( atomic ), -ish ( impish , youngish ), -ous ( hazardous ), etc.

segment.text: Adjectives may be used attributively , as part of a noun phrase (nearly always preceding the noun they modify; for exceptions see postpositive adjective ), as in the big house , or predicatively , as in the house is big .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:33176-33398", "next_segment_id": "lseg-4a1e81e2369c", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-bc11710594cf", "segment_id": "lseg-9bf31812bfec", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Adjectives may be used attributively , as part of a noun phrase (nearly always preceding the noun they modify; for exceptions see postpositive adjective ), as in the big house , or predicatively , as in the house is big ."}}

segment.text: Certain adjectives are restricted to one or other use; for example, drunken is attributive ( a drunken sailor ), while drunk is usually predicative ( the sailor was drunk ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:33398-33572", "next_segment_id": "lseg-0bf547e67ff4", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-9bf31812bfec", "segment_id": "lseg-4a1e81e2369c", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Certain adjectives are restricted to one or other use; for example, drunken is attributive ( a drunken sailor ), while drunk is usually predicative ( the sailor was drunk )."}}

segment.text: Comparison [ edit ] Many adjectives have comparative and superlative forms in -er and -est , [ 26 ] such as faster and fastest (from the positive form fast ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:33572-33731", "next_segment_id": "lseg-cbd6e4f03236", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-4a1e81e2369c", "segment_id": "lseg-0bf547e67ff4", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Comparison [ edit ] Many adjectives have comparative and superlative forms in -er and -est , [ 26 ] such as faster and fastest (from the positive form fast )."}}

segment.text: Spelling rules which maintain pronunciation apply to suffixing adjectives just as they do for similar treatment of regular past tense formation ; these cover consonant doubling (as in bigger and biggest , from big ) and the change of y to i after consonants (as in happier and happiest , from happy ).

segment.text: The adjectives good and bad have the irregular forms better, best and worse, worst ; also far becomes farther, farthest or further, furthest .

segment.text: The adjective old (for which the regular older and oldest are usual) also has the irregular forms elder and eldest , these generally being restricted to use in comparing siblings and in certain independent uses.

segment.text: Many adjectives, however, particularly those that are longer and less common, do not have inflected comparative and superlative forms.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:34438-34573", "next_segment_id": "lseg-5a47be4202a0", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-259a833ad720", "segment_id": "lseg-64e43e136143", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Many adjectives, however, particularly those that are longer and less common, do not have inflected comparative and superlative forms."}}

segment.text: Instead, they can be qualified with more and most , as in beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful (this construction is also sometimes used even for adjectives for which inflected forms do exist).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:34573-34772", "next_segment_id": "lseg-c84c056c5173", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-64e43e136143", "segment_id": "lseg-5a47be4202a0", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Instead, they can be qualified with more and most , as in beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful (this construction is also sometimes used even for adjectives for which inflected forms do exist)."}}

segment.text: Certain adjectives are classed as ungradable .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:34772-34819", "next_segment_id": "lseg-ca5a801c5678", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-5a47be4202a0", "segment_id": "lseg-c84c056c5173", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Certain adjectives are classed as ungradable ."}}

segment.text: [ 26 ] These represent properties that cannot be compared on a scale; they simply apply or do not, as with pregnant , dead , unique .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:34819-34953", "next_segment_id": "lseg-15a4fb3f331f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-c84c056c5173", "segment_id": "lseg-ca5a801c5678", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 26 ] These represent properties that cannot be compared on a scale; they simply apply or do not, as with pregnant , dead , unique ."}}

segment.text: Consequently, comparative and superlative forms of such adjectives are not normally used, except in a figurative, humorous or imprecise context.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:34953-35098", "next_segment_id": "lseg-37d5a1a9e65c", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-ca5a801c5678", "segment_id": "lseg-15a4fb3f331f", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Consequently, comparative and superlative forms of such adjectives are not normally used, except in a figurative, humorous or imprecise context."}}

segment.text: Similarly, such adjectives are not normally qualified with modifiers of degree such as very and fairly , although with some of them it is idiomatic to use adverbs such as completely .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:35098-35282", "next_segment_id": "lseg-cfd036283aa8", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-15a4fb3f331f", "segment_id": "lseg-37d5a1a9e65c", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Similarly, such adjectives are not normally qualified with modifiers of degree such as very and fairly , although with some of them it is idiomatic to use adverbs such as completely ."}}

segment.text: Another type of adjective sometimes considered ungradable is those that represent an extreme degree of some property, such as delicious and terrified .

segment.text: Phrases [ edit ] An adjective phrase is a group of words that plays the role of an adjective in a sentence.

segment.text: It usually has a single adjective as its head , to which modifiers and complements may be added.

segment.text: [ 27 ] Adjectives can be modified by a preceding adverb or adverb phrase, as in very warm , truly imposing , more than a little excited .

segment.text: Some can also be preceded by a noun or quantitative phrase, as in fat-free , two-meter-long .

segment.text: Sometimes they are used attributively after the noun , as in a woman proud of being a midwife (where they may be converted into relative clauses: a woman who is proud of being a midwife ), but it is wrong to say * a proud of being a midwife woman .

segment.text: Adverbs [ edit ] Main article: English adverbs Adverbs perform a wide range of functions.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:37176-37266", "next_segment_id": "lseg-37916dab703b", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-44e40c9dd01f", "segment_id": "lseg-12c668b74a85", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Adverbs [ edit ] Main article: English adverbs Adverbs perform a wide range of functions."}}

segment.text: They typically modify verbs (or verb phrases), adjectives (or adjectival phrases), or other adverbs (or adverbial phrases).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:37266-37390", "next_segment_id": "lseg-0c83994423ac", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-12c668b74a85", "segment_id": "lseg-37916dab703b", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "They typically modify verbs (or verb phrases), adjectives (or adjectival phrases), or other adverbs (or adverbial phrases)."}}

segment.text: [ 28 ] However, adverbs also sometimes qualify noun phrases ( only the boss ; quite a lovely place ), pronouns and determiners ( almost all ), prepositional phrases ( halfway through the movie ), or whole sentences, to provide contextual comment or indicate an attitude ( Frankly , I don't believe you ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:37390-37695", "next_segment_id": "lseg-af7c9702b233", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-37916dab703b", "segment_id": "lseg-0c83994423ac", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 28 ] However, adverbs also sometimes qualify noun phrases ( only the boss ; quite a lovely place ), pronouns and determiners ( almost all ), prepositional phrases ( halfway through the movie ), or whole sentences, to provide contextual comment or indicate an attitude ( Frankly , I don't believe you )."}}

segment.text: [ 29 ] They can also indicate a relationship between clauses or sentences ( He died, and consequently I inherited the estate ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:37695-37823", "next_segment_id": "lseg-24bb89bbcf27", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-0c83994423ac", "segment_id": "lseg-af7c9702b233", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 29 ] They can also indicate a relationship between clauses or sentences ( He died, and consequently I inherited the estate )."}}

segment.text: [ 29 ] Many English adverbs are formed from adjectives by adding the ending -ly , as in hopefully , widely , theoretically (for details of spelling and etymology, see -ly ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:37823-37997", "next_segment_id": "lseg-0ceb8b2723e7", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-af7c9702b233", "segment_id": "lseg-24bb89bbcf27", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 29 ] Many English adverbs are formed from adjectives by adding the ending -ly , as in hopefully , widely , theoretically (for details of spelling and etymology, see -ly )."}}

segment.text: Certain words can be used as both adjectives and adverbs, such as fast , straight , and hard ; these are flat adverbs .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:37997-38117", "next_segment_id": "lseg-524381f53d90", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-24bb89bbcf27", "segment_id": "lseg-0ceb8b2723e7", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Certain words can be used as both adjectives and adverbs, such as fast , straight , and hard ; these are flat adverbs ."}}

segment.text: In earlier usage more flat adverbs were accepted in formal usage; many of these survive in idioms and colloquially.

segment.text: Some suffixes that are commonly used to form adverbs from nouns are -ward[s] (as in homeward[s] ) and -wise (as in lengthwise ).

segment.text: Adverbs are also formed by adding - ly to the participles.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:38846-38905", "next_segment_id": "lseg-03b7857ab438", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-2c09994238f0", "segment_id": "lseg-4734fed0ddf2", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Adverbs are also formed by adding - ly to the participles."}}

segment.text: For example, according, a present participle adjective, becomes accordingly, an adverb, by adding - ly after it.

segment.text: However, a few adverbs retain irregular inflection for comparative and superlative forms: [ 28 ] much , more , most ; a little , less , least ; well , better , best ; badly , worse , worst ; far , further ( farther ), furthest ( farthest ); or follow the regular adjectival inflection: fast , faster , fastest ; soon , sooner , soonest ; etc.

segment.text: Adverbs indicating the manner of an action are generally placed after the verb and its objects ( We considered the proposal carefully ), although other positions are often possible ( We carefully considered the proposal ).

segment.text: (such as often , always , almost , probably , and various others such as just ) tend to be placed before the verb ( they usually have chips ), although if there is an auxiliary or other "special verb" (see § Verbs above), then the normal position for such adverbs is after that special verb (or after the first of them, if there is more than one): I have just finished the crossword ; She can usually manage a pint ; We are never late ; You might possibly have been unconscious .

segment.text: Phrases [ edit ] An adverb phrase is a phrase that acts as an adverb within a sentence.

segment.text: [ 32 ] An adverb phrase may have an adverb as its head , together with any modifiers (other adverbs or adverb phrases) and complements, analogously to the adjective phrases described above.

segment.text: The principal coordinating conjunctions in English are: and , or , but , nor , so , yet , and for .

segment.text: These can be used in many grammatical contexts to link two or more items of equal grammatical status, [ 34 ] for example: Noun phrases combined into a longer noun phrase, such as John, Eric, and Jill , the red coat or the blue one .

segment.text: [ 36 ] Some common subordinators in English are: conjunctions of time, including after , before , since , until , when , while ; conjunctions of cause and effect, including because , since , now that , as , in order that , so ; conjunctions of opposition or concession, such as although , though , even though , whereas , while ; conjunctions of condition: such as if , unless , only if , whether or not , even if , in case (that) ; the conjunction that , which produces content clauses , as well as words that produce interrogative content clauses: whether , where , when , how , etc.

segment.text: Case [ edit ] Although English has largely lost its case system, personal pronouns still have three morphological cases that are simplified forms of the nominative , objective and genitive cases : [ 37 ] The nominative case ( subjective pronouns such as I , he , she , we , they , who , whoever ), used for the subject of a finite verb and sometimes for the complement of a copula .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:47402-47785", "next_segment_id": "lseg-613de49f31f0", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-8846b73403b8", "segment_id": "lseg-dcd16c7cbf13", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Case [ edit ] Although English has largely lost its case system, personal pronouns still have three morphological cases that are simplified forms of the nominative , objective and genitive cases : [ 37 ] The nominative case ( subjective pronouns such as I , he , she , we , they , who , whoever ), used for the subject of a finite verb and sometimes for the complement of a copula ."}}

segment.text: The oblique case ( object pronouns such as me , him , her , it , us , them , whom , whomever ), used for the direct or indirect object of a verb, for the object of a preposition, for an absolute disjunct, and sometimes for the complement of a copula.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:47785-48036", "next_segment_id": "lseg-e5b4f6ec8fd0", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-dcd16c7cbf13", "segment_id": "lseg-613de49f31f0", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The oblique case ( object pronouns such as me , him , her , it , us , them , whom , whomever ), used for the direct or indirect object of a verb, for the object of a preposition, for an absolute disjunct, and sometimes for the complement of a copula."}}

segment.text: The genitive case ( possessive pronouns such as my/mine , his , her(s) , its , our(s) , their(s) , whose ), used for a grammatical possessor.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:48036-48178", "next_segment_id": "lseg-c04a4afd6bd6", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-613de49f31f0", "segment_id": "lseg-e5b4f6ec8fd0", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The genitive case ( possessive pronouns such as my/mine , his , her(s) , its , our(s) , their(s) , whose ), used for a grammatical possessor."}}

segment.text: Most English personal pronouns have five forms: the nominative and oblique case forms, the possessive case , which has both a determiner form (such as my , our ) and a distinct independent form (such as mine , ours ) (with two exceptions: the third person singular masculine and the third person singular neuter it , which use the same form for both determiner and independent [ his car , it is his ]), and a distinct reflexive or intensive form (such as myself , ourselves ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:48296-48773", "next_segment_id": "lseg-54ebdf4b4142", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-c04a4afd6bd6", "segment_id": "lseg-7013a6468b64", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Most English personal pronouns have five forms: the nominative and oblique case forms, the possessive case , which has both a determiner form (such as my , our ) and a distinct independent form (such as mine , ours ) (with two exceptions: the third person singular masculine and the third person singular neuter it , which use the same form for both determiner and independent [ his car , it is his ]), and a distinct reflexive or intensive form (such as myself , ourselves )."}}

segment.text: The interrogative personal pronoun who exhibits the greatest diversity of forms within the modern English pronoun system, having definite nominative, oblique, and genitive forms ( who , whom , whose ) and equivalently coordinating indefinite forms ( whoever , whomever , and whosever ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:48773-49060", "next_segment_id": "lseg-301b066e8382", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-7013a6468b64", "segment_id": "lseg-54ebdf4b4142", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The interrogative personal pronoun who exhibits the greatest diversity of forms within the modern English pronoun system, having definite nominative, oblique, and genitive forms ( who , whom , whose ) and equivalently coordinating indefinite forms ( whoever , whomever , and whosever )."}}

segment.text: Forms such as I , he , and we are used for the subject (" I kicked the ball"), whereas forms such as me , him and us are used for the object ("John kicked me ").

segment.text: [ 38 ] Declension [ edit ] Further information: Declension Nouns have distinct singular and plural forms; that is, they decline to reflect their grammatical number ; consider the difference between book and books .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:49222-49437", "next_segment_id": "lseg-9dacc4fddb48", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-301b066e8382", "segment_id": "lseg-7fc65a5fd27b", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 38 ] Declension [ edit ] Further information: Declension Nouns have distinct singular and plural forms; that is, they decline to reflect their grammatical number ; consider the difference between book and books ."}}

segment.text: In addition, a few English pronouns have distinct nominative (also called subjective ) and oblique (or objective) forms; that is, they decline to reflect their relationship to a verb or preposition , or case .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:49437-49647", "next_segment_id": "lseg-8561cbecadd5", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-7fc65a5fd27b", "segment_id": "lseg-9dacc4fddb48", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "In addition, a few English pronouns have distinct nominative (also called subjective ) and oblique (or objective) forms; that is, they decline to reflect their relationship to a verb or preposition , or case ."}}

segment.text: Consider the difference between he (subjective) and him (objective), as in "He saw it" and "It saw him"; similarly, consider who , which is subjective, and the objective whom .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:49647-49824", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b1a4f0979175", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-9dacc4fddb48", "segment_id": "lseg-8561cbecadd5", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Consider the difference between he (subjective) and him (objective), as in \"He saw it\" and \"It saw him\"; similarly, consider who , which is subjective, and the objective whom ."}}

segment.text: Further, these pronouns and a few others have distinct possessive forms, such as his and whose .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:49824-49921", "next_segment_id": "lseg-995e92620e1f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-8561cbecadd5", "segment_id": "lseg-b1a4f0979175", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Further, these pronouns and a few others have distinct possessive forms, such as his and whose ."}}

segment.text: By contrast, nouns have no distinct nominative and objective forms, the two being merged into a single plain case .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:49921-50037", "next_segment_id": "lseg-5e3b00125c9a", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-b1a4f0979175", "segment_id": "lseg-995e92620e1f", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "By contrast, nouns have no distinct nominative and objective forms, the two being merged into a single plain case ."}}

segment.text: For example, chair does not change form between "the chair is here" (subject) and "I saw the chair" (direct object).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:50037-50154", "next_segment_id": "lseg-12f6ace92b7f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-995e92620e1f", "segment_id": "lseg-5e3b00125c9a", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "For example, chair does not change form between \"the chair is here\" (subject) and \"I saw the chair\" (direct object)."}}

segment.text: Possession is shown by the clitic -'s attached to a possessive noun phrase , rather than by declension of the noun itself.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:50154-50277", "next_segment_id": "lseg-c3c8c8e9cf60", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-5e3b00125c9a", "segment_id": "lseg-12f6ace92b7f", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Possession is shown by the clitic -'s attached to a possessive noun phrase , rather than by declension of the noun itself."}}

segment.text: [ 39 ] Negation [ edit ] As noted above under § Verbs , a finite indicative verb (or its clause) is negated by placing the word not after an auxiliary, modal or other " special " verb such as do , can or be .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:50277-50486", "next_segment_id": "lseg-38abe7b68876", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-12f6ace92b7f", "segment_id": "lseg-c3c8c8e9cf60", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 39 ] Negation [ edit ] As noted above under § Verbs , a finite indicative verb (or its clause) is negated by placing the word not after an auxiliary, modal or other \" special \" verb such as do , can or be ."}}

segment.text: For example, the clause I go is negated with the appearance of the auxiliary do , as I do not go (see do -support ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:50486-50603", "next_segment_id": "lseg-50bc09399c94", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-c3c8c8e9cf60", "segment_id": "lseg-38abe7b68876", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "For example, the clause I go is negated with the appearance of the auxiliary do , as I do not go (see do -support )."}}

segment.text: When the affirmative already uses auxiliary verbs ( I am going ), no other auxiliary verbs are added to negate the clause ( I am not going ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:50603-50745", "next_segment_id": "lseg-42ea2ed04beb", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-38abe7b68876", "segment_id": "lseg-50bc09399c94", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "When the affirmative already uses auxiliary verbs ( I am going ), no other auxiliary verbs are added to negate the clause ( I am not going )."}}

segment.text: (Until the period of early Modern English, negation was effected without additional auxiliary verbs: I go not .
