segment.text: Clause and sentence structure [ edit ] Main article: English clause syntax A typical sentence contains one independent clause and possibly one or more dependent clauses , although it is also possible to link together sentences of this form into longer sentences, using coordinating conjunctions (see above).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:52002-52310", "next_segment_id": "lseg-8677ba3a598e", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-e5a820c77f0b", "segment_id": "lseg-61e91d58143a", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Clause and sentence structure [ edit ] Main article: English clause syntax A typical sentence contains one independent clause and possibly one or more dependent clauses , although it is also possible to link together sentences of this form into longer sentences, using coordinating conjunctions (see above)."}}

segment.text: A clause typically contains a subject (a noun phrase) and a predicate (a verb phrase in the terminology used above; that is, a verb together with its objects and complements).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:52310-52486", "next_segment_id": "lseg-4dcfd4932fa8", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-61e91d58143a", "segment_id": "lseg-8677ba3a598e", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "A clause typically contains a subject (a noun phrase) and a predicate (a verb phrase in the terminology used above; that is, a verb together with its objects and complements)."}}

segment.text: A dependent clause also normally contains a subordinating conjunction (or in the case of relative clauses, a relative pronoun, or phrase containing one).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:52486-52640", "next_segment_id": "lseg-21084ac5b5fd", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-8677ba3a598e", "segment_id": "lseg-4dcfd4932fa8", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "A dependent clause also normally contains a subordinating conjunction (or in the case of relative clauses, a relative pronoun, or phrase containing one)."}}

segment.text: Word order [ edit ] English word order has moved from the Germanic verb-second (V2) word order to being almost exclusively subject–verb–object (SVO).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:52640-52790", "next_segment_id": "lseg-03ba5708e69f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-4dcfd4932fa8", "segment_id": "lseg-21084ac5b5fd", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Word order [ edit ] English word order has moved from the Germanic verb-second (V2) word order to being almost exclusively subject–verb–object (SVO)."}}

segment.text: The combination of SVO order and use of auxiliary verbs often creates clusters of two or more verbs at the center of the sentence, such as he had hoped to try to open it .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:52790-52962", "next_segment_id": "lseg-d16db2b92057", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-21084ac5b5fd", "segment_id": "lseg-03ba5708e69f", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "The combination of SVO order and use of auxiliary verbs often creates clusters of two or more verbs at the center of the sentence, such as he had hoped to try to open it ."}}

segment.text: In most sentences, English marks grammatical relations only through word order.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:52962-53042", "next_segment_id": "lseg-93a44b4d4148", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-03ba5708e69f", "segment_id": "lseg-d16db2b92057", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "In most sentences, English marks grammatical relations only through word order."}}

segment.text: The subject constituent precedes the verb and the object constituent follows it.

segment.text: [ 40 ] Questions [ edit ] Like many other Western European languages, English historically allowed questions to be formed by inverting the positions of the verb and subject .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:53363-53538", "next_segment_id": "lseg-13ea4ec958a1", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-5aae5949f34f", "segment_id": "lseg-a6495a2fbda9", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 40 ] Questions [ edit ] Like many other Western European languages, English historically allowed questions to be formed by inverting the positions of the verb and subject ."}}

segment.text: Modern English permits this only in the case of a small class of verbs (" special verbs "), consisting of auxiliaries as well as forms of the copula be (see subject–auxiliary inversion ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:53538-53726", "next_segment_id": "lseg-cddbd20d6a87", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-a6495a2fbda9", "segment_id": "lseg-13ea4ec958a1", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Modern English permits this only in the case of a small class of verbs (\" special verbs \"), consisting of auxiliaries as well as forms of the copula be (see subject–auxiliary inversion )."}}

segment.text: To form a question from a sentence which does not have such an auxiliary or copula present, the auxiliary verb do ( does , did ) needs to be inserted, along with inversion of the word order, to form a question (see do -support ).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:53726-53956", "next_segment_id": "lseg-0dbb36c70f8a", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-13ea4ec958a1", "segment_id": "lseg-cddbd20d6a87", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "To form a question from a sentence which does not have such an auxiliary or copula present, the auxiliary verb do ( does , did ) needs to be inserted, along with inversion of the word order, to form a question (see do -support )."}}

segment.text: Indirect yes–no questions can be expressed using if or whether as the interrogative word: Ask them whether/if they saw him .

segment.text: Negative questions are formed similarly; however, if the verb undergoing inversion has a contraction with not , then it is possible to invert the subject with this contraction as a whole.

segment.text: Dependent clauses [ edit ] The syntax of a dependent clause is generally the same as that of an independent clause, except that the dependent clause usually begins with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun (or phrase containing such).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:55444-55690", "next_segment_id": "lseg-41221148a264", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-3d48825f9a35", "segment_id": "lseg-a8bbd2851869", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Dependent clauses [ edit ] The syntax of a dependent clause is generally the same as that of an independent clause, except that the dependent clause usually begins with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun (or phrase containing such)."}}

segment.text: In some situations (as already described) the conjunction or relative pronoun that can be omitted.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:55690-55789", "next_segment_id": "lseg-68f3b9f6211a", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-a8bbd2851869", "segment_id": "lseg-41221148a264", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "In some situations (as already described) the conjunction or relative pronoun that can be omitted."}}

segment.text: Another type of dependent clause with no subordinating conjunction is the conditional clause formed by inversion (see below).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:55789-55915", "next_segment_id": "lseg-a6d0b5d5e40f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-41221148a264", "segment_id": "lseg-68f3b9f6211a", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Another type of dependent clause with no subordinating conjunction is the conditional clause formed by inversion (see below)."}}

segment.text: Other uses of inversion [ edit ] The clause structure with an inverted subject and verb, used to form questions as described above, is also used in certain types of declarative sentences.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:55915-56103", "next_segment_id": "lseg-80d12412dd9f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-68f3b9f6211a", "segment_id": "lseg-a6d0b5d5e40f", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "Other uses of inversion [ edit ] The clause structure with an inverted subject and verb, used to form questions as described above, is also used in certain types of declarative sentences."}}

segment.text: This occurs mainly when the sentence begins with adverbial or other phrases that are essentially negative or contain words such as only , hardly , etc.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:56103-56255", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b8fb5c535357", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-a6d0b5d5e40f", "segment_id": "lseg-80d12412dd9f", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "This occurs mainly when the sentence begins with adverbial or other phrases that are essentially negative or contain words such as only , hardly , etc."}}

segment.text: : Never have I known someone so stupid; Only in France can such food be tasted .

segment.text: In elliptical sentences (see below), inversion takes place after so (meaning "also") as well as after the negative neither : so do I, neither does she .

segment.text: Inversion can also be used to form conditional clauses, beginning with should , were (subjunctive), or had , in the following ways: should I win the race (equivalent to if I should win the race ); were he a soldier (equivalent to if he were a soldier ); were he to win the race (equivalent to if he were to win the race , i.

segment.text: Imperatives [ edit ] In an imperative sentence (one giving an order), there is usually no subject in the independent clause: Go away until I call you .

segment.text: It is possible, however, to include you as the subject for emphasis: You stay away from me .

segment.text: Some notable elliptical forms found in English include: Short statements of the form I can , he isn't , we mustn't .

segment.text: History of English grammars [ edit ] Main article: History of English grammars The first published English grammar was a Pamphlet for Grammar of 1586, written by William Bullokar with the stated goal of demonstrating that English was just as rule-based as Latin.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:58368-58631", "next_segment_id": "lseg-e6be26a6e922", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-28d1ee4543ae", "segment_id": "lseg-43c9c12f0804", "source_id": "lsource-44335ac3a9bd", "start_time": null, "text": "History of English grammars [ edit ] Main article: History of English grammars The first published English grammar was a Pamphlet for Grammar of 1586, written by William Bullokar with the stated goal of demonstrating that English was just as rule-based as Latin."}}

segment.text: Bullokar's grammar was faithfully modeled on William Lily's Latin grammar, Rudimenta Grammatices (1534), used in English schools at that time, having been "prescribed" for them in 1542 by Henry VIII .

segment.text: Bullokar wrote his grammar in English and used a "reformed spelling system" of his own invention; but much English grammar, for much of the century after Bullokar's effort, was written in Latin, especially by authors who were aiming to be scholarly.

source.title: El subjuntivo en espanol - C1 level

idempotency_key: language.source.imported:{"source": {"attachment_manifest": {}, "content_hash": "cb6693561d38e93819384ab587893eeeee7e47fea05efca4e12fc15b0a8cae0c", "duration_seconds": null, "imported_at": "2026-06-02T06:20:57.537980+00:00", "language": "es", "source_id": "lsource-44b51f4b63eb", "source_type": "resource", "title": "El subjuntivo en espanol - C1 level", "url": "https://es.wikibooks.org/wiki/Espanol/Subjuntivo"}}

language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:0-25", "next_segment_id": "lseg-dace57798142", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "", "segment_id": "lseg-860e2262fc7d", "source_id": "lsource-44b51f4b63eb", "start_time": null, "text": "El subjuntivo en espanol."}}

segment.text: El modo subjuntivo es fundamental para expresar subjetividad.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:25-87", "next_segment_id": "lseg-6e908c4c2e7d", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-860e2262fc7d", "segment_id": "lseg-dace57798142", "source_id": "lsource-44b51f4b63eb", "start_time": null, "text": "El modo subjuntivo es fundamental para expresar subjetividad."}}

segment.text: Se utiliza en situaciones de duda, deseo, emocion, necesidad, opinion negativa o hipotesis.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:87-179", "next_segment_id": "lseg-657904fdbce0", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-dace57798142", "segment_id": "lseg-6e908c4c2e7d", "source_id": "lsource-44b51f4b63eb", "start_time": null, "text": "Se utiliza en situaciones de duda, deseo, emocion, necesidad, opinion negativa o hipotesis."}}

segment.text: Las conjunciones como que, cuando, aunque introducen el subjuntivo.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:179-247", "next_segment_id": "lseg-fd0c05692b26", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-6e908c4c2e7d", "segment_id": "lseg-657904fdbce0", "source_id": "lsource-44b51f4b63eb", "start_time": null, "text": "Las conjunciones como que, cuando, aunque introducen el subjuntivo."}}

language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:247-283", "next_segment_id": "lseg-27304b9e92e1", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-657904fdbce0", "segment_id": "lseg-fd0c05692b26", "source_id": "lsource-44b51f4b63eb", "start_time": null, "text": "Ejemplos: Espero que vengas manana."}}

language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:283-304", "next_segment_id": "lseg-e195c7acf3d0", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-fd0c05692b26", "segment_id": "lseg-27304b9e92e1", "source_id": "lsource-44b51f4b63eb", "start_time": null, "text": "Dudo que sea verdad."}}

language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:304-332", "next_segment_id": "lseg-7866ce23127b", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-27304b9e92e1", "segment_id": "lseg-e195c7acf3d0", "source_id": "lsource-44b51f4b63eb", "start_time": null, "text": "Es importante que estudies."}}

segment.text: El imperfecto de subjuntivo tiene dos terminaciones: -ra y -se.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:332-396", "next_segment_id": "lseg-57bebf5227b6", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-e195c7acf3d0", "segment_id": "lseg-7866ce23127b", "source_id": "lsource-44b51f4b63eb", "start_time": null, "text": "El imperfecto de subjuntivo tiene dos terminaciones: -ra y -se."}}

segment.text: Si estudiara o estudiase mas, aprobaria.

segment.text: El modo subjuntivo es un modo gramatical que expresa la subjetividad del hablante.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:30-113", "next_segment_id": "lseg-75afa61ff5d7", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-28299ead4849", "segment_id": "lseg-aa1d306ff2df", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "El modo subjuntivo es un modo gramatical que expresa la subjetividad del hablante."}}

segment.text: A diferencia del indicativo, que expresa hechos objetivos, el subjuntivo se utiliza para expresar dudas, deseos, emociones, opiniones personales y situaciones hipoteticas.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:113-285", "next_segment_id": "lseg-e1fbb5f39655", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-aa1d306ff2df", "segment_id": "lseg-75afa61ff5d7", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "A diferencia del indicativo, que expresa hechos objetivos, el subjuntivo se utiliza para expresar dudas, deseos, emociones, opiniones personales y situaciones hipoteticas."}}

segment.text: Los usos principales del subjuntivo incluyen: 1) Expresar deseos: Ojala que llueva cafe.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:285-374", "next_segment_id": "lseg-48e1033cc68a", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-75afa61ff5d7", "segment_id": "lseg-e1fbb5f39655", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "Los usos principales del subjuntivo incluyen: 1) Expresar deseos: Ojala que llueva cafe."}}

segment.text: 2) Expresar emociones: Me alegra que estes aqui.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:374-423", "next_segment_id": "lseg-1dbb717124bd", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-e1fbb5f39655", "segment_id": "lseg-48e1033cc68a", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "2) Expresar emociones: Me alegra que estes aqui."}}

language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:423-458", "next_segment_id": "lseg-ad43d182f0df", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-48e1033cc68a", "segment_id": "lseg-1dbb717124bd", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "3) Expresar dudas: Dudo que venga."}}

segment.text: 4) Expresar necesidad: Es necesario que hables.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:458-506", "next_segment_id": "lseg-14323743c8f9", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-1dbb717124bd", "segment_id": "lseg-ad43d182f0df", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "4) Expresar necesidad: Es necesario que hables."}}

segment.text: 5) Expresar opinion negativa: No creo que sea cierto.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:506-560", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b262dd71fe23", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-ad43d182f0df", "segment_id": "lseg-14323743c8f9", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "5) Expresar opinion negativa: No creo que sea cierto."}}

segment.text: El presente de subjuntivo se forma tomando la primera persona del singular del presente de indicativo, eliminando la -o y anadiendo las terminaciones opuestas: para verbos -ar: -e, -es, -e, -emos, -eis, -en.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:560-768", "next_segment_id": "lseg-464091130302", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-14323743c8f9", "segment_id": "lseg-b262dd71fe23", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "El presente de subjuntivo se forma tomando la primera persona del singular del presente de indicativo, eliminando la -o y anadiendo las terminaciones opuestas: para verbos -ar: -e, -es, -e, -emos, -eis, -en."}}

language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:768-820", "next_segment_id": "lseg-e8d7088cc5fd", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-b262dd71fe23", "segment_id": "lseg-464091130302", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "Para verbos -er/-ir: -a, -as, -a, -amos, -ais, -an."}}

segment.text: El imperfecto de subjuntivo tiene dos formas: la forma -ra (cantara, comiera, viviera) y la forma -se (cantase, comiese, viviese).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:820-951", "next_segment_id": "lseg-763bee43e7ee", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-464091130302", "segment_id": "lseg-e8d7088cc5fd", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "El imperfecto de subjuntivo tiene dos formas: la forma -ra (cantara, comiera, viviera) y la forma -se (cantase, comiese, viviese)."}}

segment.text: La forma -ra es mas comun en el espanol actual, mientras que la forma -se se usa mas en contextos literarios o formales.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:951-1072", "next_segment_id": "lseg-9a6913e57993", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-e8d7088cc5fd", "segment_id": "lseg-763bee43e7ee", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "La forma -ra es mas comun en el espanol actual, mientras que la forma -se se usa mas en contextos literarios o formales."}}

segment.text: El pluscuamperfecto de subjuntivo se forma con el imperfecto de subjuntivo del verbo haber mas el participio: hubiera/hubiese hablado, hubieras/hubieses comido.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1072-1233", "next_segment_id": "lseg-17dee6ddff36", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-763bee43e7ee", "segment_id": "lseg-9a6913e57993", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "El pluscuamperfecto de subjuntivo se forma con el imperfecto de subjuntivo del verbo haber mas el participio: hubiera/hubiese hablado, hubieras/hubieses comido."}}

segment.text: Las conjunciones que requieren subjuntivo incluyen: antes de que, para que, a fin de que, sin que, con tal de que, a menos que, en caso de que, siempre y cuando, mientras que.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1233-1409", "next_segment_id": "lseg-84a8cd1246be", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-9a6913e57993", "segment_id": "lseg-17dee6ddff36", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "Las conjunciones que requieren subjuntivo incluyen: antes de que, para que, a fin de que, sin que, con tal de que, a menos que, en caso de que, siempre y cuando, mientras que."}}

segment.text: Usos del subjuntivo en clausulas adjetivas: Busco un profesor que hable espanol nativo.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1409-1497", "next_segment_id": "lseg-0208d86d285e", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-17dee6ddff36", "segment_id": "lseg-84a8cd1246be", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "Usos del subjuntivo en clausulas adjetivas: Busco un profesor que hable espanol nativo."}}

segment.text: No hay nadie que sepa la respuesta.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1497-1533", "next_segment_id": "lseg-c5012bce99b9", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-84a8cd1246be", "segment_id": "lseg-0208d86d285e", "source_id": "lsource-f6aad9d1ffcc", "start_time": null, "text": "No hay nadie que sepa la respuesta."}}

segment.text: Usos del subjuntivo en clausulas adverbiales: Cuando llegues, llamame.

segment.text: Los modismos son expresiones idiomaticas cuyo significado no es literal.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:24-97", "next_segment_id": "lseg-4321685df7a9", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-c0e54dec2d69", "segment_id": "lseg-4c4fda140975", "source_id": "lsource-621e2c23b296", "start_time": null, "text": "Los modismos son expresiones idiomaticas cuyo significado no es literal."}}

segment.text: Son fundamentales para alcanzar un nivel C1 de competencia linguistica.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:97-169", "next_segment_id": "lseg-204849591c7f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-4c4fda140975", "segment_id": "lseg-4321685df7a9", "source_id": "lsource-621e2c23b296", "start_time": null, "text": "Son fundamentales para alcanzar un nivel C1 de competencia linguistica."}}

segment.text:
Los siguientes modismos son de uso frecuente en el espanol avanzado:
1) Estar en las nubes - Significa estar distraido o no prestar atencion.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:169-311", "next_segment_id": "lseg-0e535dddfaf3", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-4321685df7a9", "segment_id": "lseg-204849591c7f", "source_id": "lsource-621e2c23b296", "start_time": null, "text": "Los siguientes modismos son de uso frecuente en el espanol avanzado:\n1) Estar en las nubes - Significa estar distraido o no prestar atencion."}}

segment.text: Ejemplo: Juan esta en las nubes, no escucha nada.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:311-361", "next_segment_id": "lseg-2b29673cca68", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-204849591c7f", "segment_id": "lseg-0e535dddfaf3", "source_id": "lsource-621e2c23b296", "start_time": null, "text": "Ejemplo: Juan esta en las nubes, no escucha nada."}}

segment.text: 2) Tirar la toalla - Significa rendirse o abandonar.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:361-414", "next_segment_id": "lseg-0487b7be255a", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-0e535dddfaf3", "segment_id": "lseg-2b29673cca68", "source_id": "lsource-621e2c23b296", "start_time": null, "text": "2) Tirar la toalla - Significa rendirse o abandonar."}}

segment.text: Ejemplo: Despues de varios intentos, tiro la toalla.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:414-467", "next_segment_id": "lseg-48e1fec048d9", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-2b29673cca68", "segment_id": "lseg-0487b7be255a", "source_id": "lsource-621e2c23b296", "start_time": null, "text": "Ejemplo: Despues de varios intentos, tiro la toalla."}}

segment.text: 3) Ser pan comido - Significa ser muy facil.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:467-512", "next_segment_id": "lseg-fe328bf40018", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-0487b7be255a", "segment_id": "lseg-48e1fec048d9", "source_id": "lsource-621e2c23b296", "start_time": null, "text": "3) Ser pan comido - Significa ser muy facil."}}

segment.text: Ejemplo: Este examen es pan comido.

segment.text: 4) Meter la pata - Significa cometer un error o equivocacion.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:548-610", "next_segment_id": "lseg-e520095bf4bd", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-fe328bf40018", "segment_id": "lseg-1f43cfa120b1", "source_id": "lsource-621e2c23b296", "start_time": null, "text": "4) Meter la pata - Significa cometer un error o equivocacion."}}

segment.text: 5) Costar un ojo de la cara - Significa ser muy caro.

segment.text: 6) Estar como una cabra - Significa estar loco.

segment.text: 7) No tener pelos en la lengua - Significa ser directo y sincero.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:840-906", "next_segment_id": "lseg-82387276d63e", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-cd55a89aed13", "segment_id": "lseg-48de3a2eef99", "source_id": "lsource-621e2c23b296", "start_time": null, "text": "7) No tener pelos en la lengua - Significa ser directo y sincero."}}

language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:974-1012", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b1947330ab95", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-82387276d63e", "segment_id": "lseg-8a34e2c49593", "source_id": "lsource-621e2c23b296", "start_time": null, "text": "8) Echar una mano - Significa ayudar."}}

segment.text: 9) Ponerse las pilas - Significa empezar a actuar con energia.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1056-1119", "next_segment_id": "lseg-339313e356c4", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-b1947330ab95", "segment_id": "lseg-0040c65f97e9", "source_id": "lsource-621e2c23b296", "start_time": null, "text": "9) Ponerse las pilas - Significa empezar a actuar con energia."}}

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1265-1332", "next_segment_id": "lseg-57bf9cfef858", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-a8fea4c82097", "segment_id": "lseg-253e6f292604", "source_id": "lsource-621e2c23b296", "start_time": null, "text": "11) Hacer la vista gorda - Significa ignorar algo deliberadamente."}}

segment.text: [ 4 ] [ 5 ] [ 6 ] The namesake of the language is the Angles , one of the Germanic peoples who migrated to Britain after the end of Roman rule .

segment.text: Primary dialect regions in the United Kingdom and Ireland The fact that English has been spoken in England for 1,500 years explains why England has a great wealth of regional dialects.

segment.text: [ 145 ] Within the United Kingdom, Received Pronunciation (RP), an educated accent associated originally with South East England , has been traditionally used as a broadcast standard and is considered the most prestigious of British accents.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:37961-38203", "next_segment_id": "lseg-dc31df9dd5ab", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-99c2191788d6", "segment_id": "lseg-22431e3d7532", "source_id": "lsource-e4255926bcd4", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 145 ] Within the United Kingdom, Received Pronunciation (RP), an educated accent associated originally with South East England , has been traditionally used as a broadcast standard and is considered the most prestigious of British accents."}}

segment.text: The spread of RP (also known as BBC English) through the media has caused many traditional dialects of rural England to recede, as youths adopt the traits of the prestige variety instead of traits from local dialects.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:38203-38421", "next_segment_id": "lseg-69b99c5450f4", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-22431e3d7532", "segment_id": "lseg-dc31df9dd5ab", "source_id": "lsource-e4255926bcd4", "start_time": null, "text": "The spread of RP (also known as BBC English) through the media has caused many traditional dialects of rural England to recede, as youths adopt the traits of the prestige variety instead of traits from local dialects."}}

segment.text: At the time of the 1950–61 Survey of English Dialects , grammar and vocabulary differed across the country, but a process of lexical attrition has led most of this variation to disappear.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:38421-38609", "next_segment_id": "lseg-9a1c5e869d72", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-dc31df9dd5ab", "segment_id": "lseg-69b99c5450f4", "source_id": "lsource-e4255926bcd4", "start_time": null, "text": "At the time of the 1950–61 Survey of English Dialects , grammar and vocabulary differed across the country, but a process of lexical attrition has led most of this variation to disappear."}}

segment.text: [ 146 ] Nonetheless, this attrition has mostly affected dialectal variation in grammar and vocabulary.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:38609-38712", "next_segment_id": "lseg-bfa345ae432b", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-69b99c5450f4", "segment_id": "lseg-9a1c5e869d72", "source_id": "lsource-e4255926bcd4", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 146 ] Nonetheless, this attrition has mostly affected dialectal variation in grammar and vocabulary."}}

segment.text: Only 3% of the English population actually speak RP, the remainder speaking in regional accents and dialects with varying degrees of RP influence.

segment.text: [ 147 ] There is also variability within RP, particularly along class lines between Upper and Middle-class RP speakers and between native RP speakers and speakers who adopt RP later in life.

segment.text: [ 148 ] Within Britain, there is also considerable variation along lines of social class; some traits, though exceedingly common, are nonetheless considered "non-standard" and associated with lower-class speakers and identities.

segment.text: An example of this is h -dropping , which was historically a feature of lower-class London English, particularly Cockney, and can now be heard in the local accents of most parts of England.

segment.text: However, it remains largely absent in broadcasting and among the upper crust of British society.

segment.text: [ 149 ] English in England can be divided into four major dialect regions: South East English, South West English (also known as West Country English ), Midlands English and Northern English .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:39566-39759", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b22bf6398778", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-ebb9d6b19a49", "segment_id": "lseg-86c7928771c3", "source_id": "lsource-e4255926bcd4", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 149 ] English in England can be divided into four major dialect regions: South East English, South West English (also known as West Country English ), Midlands English and Northern English ."}}

segment.text: Within each of these regions, several local dialects exist: within the Northern region, there is a division between the Yorkshire dialects , the Geordie dialect (spoken around Newcastle , in Northumbria ) and the Lancashire dialects, which include the urban subdialects of Manchester ( Mancunian ) and Liverpool ( Scouse ).

segment.text: Having been the centre of Danish occupation during the Viking invasions of England, Northern English dialects, particularly the Yorkshire dialect, retain Norse features not found in other English varieties.

segment.text: [ 150 ] In the West Midlands , dialects such as Black Country ( Yam Yam ), and by less extent Birmingham ( Brummie ), preserve archaic features from early modern and Middle English, retaining Germanic elements such as specific grammatical structures and vocabulary.

segment.text: [ 151 ] Since the 15th century, South East England varieties have centred on London, which has been the centre from which dialectal innovations have spread to other dialects.

segment.text: In London, the Cockney dialect was traditionally used by the lower classes, and it was long a socially stigmatised variety.

segment.text: The spread of Cockney features across the South East led the media to talk of Estuary English as a new dialect, but the notion was criticised by many linguists on the grounds that London had been influencing neighbouring regions throughout history.

segment.text: Phonological variation affects the inventory of phonemes (speech sounds that distinguish meaning), and phonetic variation consists in differences in pronunciation of the phonemes.

segment.text: Fortis obstruents, such as /p tʃ s/ are pronounced with more muscular tension and breath force than lenis consonants, such as /b dʒ z/ , and are always voiceless .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:55562-55726", "next_segment_id": "lseg-192aed6f3de6", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-2aa1a945bf51", "segment_id": "lseg-a6afca14caf9", "source_id": "lsource-e4255926bcd4", "start_time": null, "text": "Fortis obstruents, such as /p tʃ s/ are pronounced with more muscular tension and breath force than lenis consonants, such as /b dʒ z/ , and are always voiceless ."}}

segment.text: Lenis consonants are partly voiced at the beginning and end of utterances, and fully voiced between vowels.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:55726-55834", "next_segment_id": "lseg-c796b70909e3", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-a6afca14caf9", "segment_id": "lseg-192aed6f3de6", "source_id": "lsource-e4255926bcd4", "start_time": null, "text": "Lenis consonants are partly voiced at the beginning and end of utterances, and fully voiced between vowels."}}

segment.text: Fortis stops such as /p/ have additional articulatory or acoustic features in most dialects: they are aspirated [pʰ] when they occur alone at the beginning of a stressed syllable, often unaspirated in other cases, and often unreleased [p̚] or pre-glottalised [ʔp] at the end of a syllable.

segment.text: [ 212 ] In both RP and GA, vowels are phonetically shortened before fortis consonants in the same syllable , like /t tʃ f/ , but not before lenis consonants like /d dʒ v/ or in open syllables: thus, the vowels of rich [rɪtʃ] , neat [nit] , and safe [seɪ̯f] are noticeably shorter than the vowels of ridge [rɪˑdʒ] , need [niˑd] , and save [seˑɪ̯v] , and the vowel of light [laɪ̯t] is shorter than that of lie [laˑɪ̯] .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:57955-58373", "next_segment_id": "lseg-7bb8fd2008fe", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-51cb0bf6234c", "segment_id": "lseg-d0dc45432155", "source_id": "lsource-e4255926bcd4", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 212 ] In both RP and GA, vowels are phonetically shortened before fortis consonants in the same syllable , like /t tʃ f/ , but not before lenis consonants like /d dʒ v/ or in open syllables: thus, the vowels of rich [rɪtʃ] , neat [nit] , and safe [seɪ̯f] are noticeably shorter than the vowels of ridge [rɪˑdʒ] , need [niˑd] , and save [seˑɪ̯v] , and the vowel of light [laɪ̯t] is shorter than that of lie [laˑɪ̯] ."}}

segment.text: Because lenis consonants are frequently voiceless at the end of a syllable, vowel length is an important cue as to whether the following consonant is lenis or fortis.

segment.text: [ 213 ] The vowel /ə/ only occurs in unstressed syllables and is more open in quality in stem-final positions.

segment.text: [ 214 ] [ 215 ] Some dialects do not contrast /ɪ/ and /ə/ in unstressed positions, such that rabbit and abbot rhyme and Lenin and Lennon are homophonous, a dialectal feature called the weak vowel merger .

segment.text: Syllable onset and coda (start and end) are optional.

segment.text: A syllable can start with up to three consonant sounds, as in sprint /sprɪnt/ , and end with up to five, as in (for some dialects) angsts /aŋksts/ .

segment.text: Certain syllables are stressed, while others are unstressed.

segment.text: Stress is a combination of duration, intensity, vowel quality, and sometimes changes in pitch.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:60493-60588", "next_segment_id": "lseg-267d88cf1eca", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-0b223a81ec85", "segment_id": "lseg-c01e846df6b5", "source_id": "lsource-e4255926bcd4", "start_time": null, "text": "Stress is a combination of duration, intensity, vowel quality, and sometimes changes in pitch."}}

segment.text: Stressed syllables are pronounced longer and louder than unstressed syllables, and vowels in unstressed syllables are frequently reduced while vowels in stressed syllables are not.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:60588-60769", "next_segment_id": "lseg-241ec12455fc", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-c01e846df6b5", "segment_id": "lseg-267d88cf1eca", "source_id": "lsource-e4255926bcd4", "start_time": null, "text": "Stressed syllables are pronounced longer and louder than unstressed syllables, and vowels in unstressed syllables are frequently reduced while vowels in stressed syllables are not."}}

segment.text: [ 220 ] Stress in English is phonemic , gaining freedom and dynamicity once lost in Proto-Germanic through a majority of borrowings from non-Germanic languages.

segment.text: [ 227 ] English has undergone many historical sound changes , some of them affecting all varieties, and others affecting only a few.

segment.text: Most standard varieties are affected by the Great Vowel Shift , which changed the pronunciation of long vowels, but a few dialects have slightly different results.

segment.text: [ 237 ] Although letters and speech sounds do not have a one-to-one correspondence in standard English spelling, spelling rules that take into account syllable structure, phonetic changes in derived words, and word accent are reliable for most English words.

segment.text: [ 294 ] The subject constituent precedes the verb and the object constituent follows it.

segment.text: The grammatical roles of each constituent are marked only by the position relative to the verb: S V O The dog bites the man The man bites the dog An exception is found in sentences where one of the constituents is a pronoun, in which case it is doubly marked, both by word order and by case inflection, where the subject pronoun precedes the verb and takes the subjective case form, and the object pronoun follows the verb and takes the objective case form.

segment.text: Within a sentence, there is always at least one main clause (or matrix clause) whereas other clauses are subordinate to a main clause.

segment.text: Subordinate clauses may function as arguments of the verb in the main clause.

segment.text: For example, in the phrase "I think (that) you are lying", the main clause is headed by the verb think , the subject is I , but the object of the phrase is the subordinate clause "(that) you are lying".

segment.text: [ 297 ] Relative clauses are clauses that function as a modifier or specifier to some constituent in the main clause: For example, in the sentence "I saw the letter that you received today", the relative clause "that you received today" specifies the meaning of the word letter , the object of the main clause.

segment.text: Relative clauses can be introduced by the pronouns who , whose , whom , and which as well as by that (which can also be omitted).

segment.text: They are formed by using the past participle either with the auxiliary verb to be or to get , although not all varieties of English allow the use of passives with get .

segment.text: [ 306 ] Focus constructions emphasise a particular piece of new or salient information within a sentence, generally through allocating the main sentence level stress on the focal constituent.

segment.text: For example, "the girl was stung by a bee " (emphasising it was a bee and not, for example, a wasp that stung her), or " the girl was stung by a bee" (contrasting with another possibility, for example that it was the boy).

segment.text: The target readership is English as a second or foreign language students intending to enter English-medium higher education , and teachers of such students.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1091-1249", "next_segment_id": "lseg-739e92fe35ca", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-b67de90cd3c0", "segment_id": "lseg-11c5b87f1a5a", "source_id": "lsource-87e3d851fdaf", "start_time": null, "text": "The target readership is English as a second or foreign language students intending to enter English-medium higher education , and teachers of such students."}}

segment.text: The AWL was developed by Averil Coxhead at the School of Linguistics and Applied Language Studies at Victoria University of Wellington , New Zealand.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1249-1399", "next_segment_id": "lseg-a254cc8068d4", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-11c5b87f1a5a", "segment_id": "lseg-739e92fe35ca", "source_id": "lsource-87e3d851fdaf", "start_time": null, "text": "The AWL was developed by Averil Coxhead at the School of Linguistics and Applied Language Studies at Victoria University of Wellington , New Zealand."}}

segment.text: This list replaced the previously widely used University Word List , developed by Xue and Nation in 1986.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1399-1505", "next_segment_id": "lseg-5e6b511de698", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-739e92fe35ca", "segment_id": "lseg-a254cc8068d4", "source_id": "lsource-87e3d851fdaf", "start_time": null, "text": "This list replaced the previously widely used University Word List , developed by Xue and Nation in 1986."}}

segment.text: The words included in the AWL were selected based on their range (breadth of academic areas covered), frequency, and dispersion (uniformity of frequency), [ 2 ] and were divided into ten sublists, each containing 1000 words in decreasing order of frequency.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1505-1763", "next_segment_id": "lseg-41678ac03471", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-a254cc8068d4", "segment_id": "lseg-5e6b511de698", "source_id": "lsource-87e3d851fdaf", "start_time": null, "text": "The words included in the AWL were selected based on their range (breadth of academic areas covered), frequency, and dispersion (uniformity of frequency), [ 2 ] and were divided into ten sublists, each containing 1000 words in decreasing order of frequency."}}

segment.text: The AWL excludes words from the General Service List (the 2000 highest-frequency words in general texts).

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1763-1869", "next_segment_id": "lseg-772542f87e62", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-5e6b511de698", "segment_id": "lseg-41678ac03471", "source_id": "lsource-87e3d851fdaf", "start_time": null, "text": "The AWL excludes words from the General Service List (the 2000 highest-frequency words in general texts)."}}

segment.text: Many words in the AWL are general vocabulary not restricted to an academic domain, such as the words area , approach , create , similar , and occur, found in Sublist One, and the AWL only accounts for a small percentage of the actual word occurrences in academic texts.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1869-2139", "next_segment_id": "lseg-90c7a8a07461", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-41678ac03471", "segment_id": "lseg-772542f87e62", "source_id": "lsource-87e3d851fdaf", "start_time": null, "text": "Many words in the AWL are general vocabulary not restricted to an academic domain, such as the words area , approach , create , similar , and occur, found in Sublist One, and the AWL only accounts for a small percentage of the actual word occurrences in academic texts."}}

segment.text: [ 3 ] In the second decade of the twenty-first century, a revised list, called the New Academic Word List (NAWL), was developed and made public.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2139-2284", "next_segment_id": "lseg-73e481910f52", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-772542f87e62", "segment_id": "lseg-90c7a8a07461", "source_id": "lsource-87e3d851fdaf", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 3 ] In the second decade of the twenty-first century, a revised list, called the New Academic Word List (NAWL), was developed and made public."}}

segment.text: [ 4 ] This list is available on the Simple English Wiktionary .

segment.text: The Academic Vocabulary List , based on the Academic Word List, drawing from the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA), was developed by Gardner and Davies in 2013.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2348-2522", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b1e985882bdf", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-73e481910f52", "segment_id": "lseg-6d932aed3292", "source_id": "lsource-87e3d851fdaf", "start_time": null, "text": "The Academic Vocabulary List , based on the Academic Word List, drawing from the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA), was developed by Gardner and Davies in 2013."}}

segment.text: Rather than relying on word families , like the AWL, the AVL is composed of 3000 English lemmas , and provides a broader coverage of Academic English.

segment.text: In corpus linguistics , a collocation is a series of words or terms that co-occur more often than would be expected by chance.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1356-1483", "next_segment_id": "lseg-428e71e3f5c0", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-71789c6a7f4a", "segment_id": "lseg-ccff0255cd02", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "In corpus linguistics , a collocation is a series of words or terms that co-occur more often than would be expected by chance."}}

segment.text: In phraseology , a collocation is a type of compositional phraseme , meaning that it can be understood from the words that make it up.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1483-1618", "next_segment_id": "lseg-35d103052ace", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-ccff0255cd02", "segment_id": "lseg-428e71e3f5c0", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "In phraseology , a collocation is a type of compositional phraseme , meaning that it can be understood from the words that make it up."}}

segment.text: This contrasts with an idiom , where the meaning of the whole cannot be inferred from its parts, and may be completely unrelated.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1618-1748", "next_segment_id": "lseg-25d3d1a9f776", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-428e71e3f5c0", "segment_id": "lseg-35d103052ace", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "This contrasts with an idiom , where the meaning of the whole cannot be inferred from its parts, and may be completely unrelated."}}

segment.text: There are about seven main types of collocations: adjective + noun, noun + noun (such as collective nouns ), noun + verb, verb + noun, adverb + adjective, verbs + prepositional phrase ( phrasal verbs ), and verb + adverb.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1748-1970", "next_segment_id": "lseg-e16dec625563", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-35d103052ace", "segment_id": "lseg-25d3d1a9f776", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "There are about seven main types of collocations: adjective + noun, noun + noun (such as collective nouns ), noun + verb, verb + noun, adverb + adjective, verbs + prepositional phrase ( phrasal verbs ), and verb + adverb."}}

segment.text: Collocation extraction is a computational technique that finds collocations in a document or corpus, using various computational linguistics elements resembling data mining .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1970-2145", "next_segment_id": "lseg-7051f4e5f7a7", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-25d3d1a9f776", "segment_id": "lseg-e16dec625563", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "Collocation extraction is a computational technique that finds collocations in a document or corpus, using various computational linguistics elements resembling data mining ."}}

segment.text: Expanded definition [ edit ] Collocations are partly or fully fixed expressions that become established through repeated context-dependent use.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2145-2289", "next_segment_id": "lseg-3ee34233e172", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-e16dec625563", "segment_id": "lseg-7051f4e5f7a7", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "Expanded definition [ edit ] Collocations are partly or fully fixed expressions that become established through repeated context-dependent use."}}

segment.text: Such terms as crystal clear , middle management , nuclear family , and cosmetic surgery are examples of collocated pairs of words.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2289-2420", "next_segment_id": "lseg-8b7ed20a5f92", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-7051f4e5f7a7", "segment_id": "lseg-3ee34233e172", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "Such terms as crystal clear , middle management , nuclear family , and cosmetic surgery are examples of collocated pairs of words."}}

segment.text: Collocations can be in a syntactic relation (such as verb–object : make and decision ), lexical relation (such as antonymy ), or they can be in no linguistically defined relation.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2420-2600", "next_segment_id": "lseg-68d4d231519f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-3ee34233e172", "segment_id": "lseg-8b7ed20a5f92", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "Collocations can be in a syntactic relation (such as verb–object : make and decision ), lexical relation (such as antonymy ), or they can be in no linguistically defined relation."}}

segment.text: Knowledge of collocations is vital for the competent use of a language: a grammatically correct sentence will stand out as awkward if collocational preferences are violated.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2600-2774", "next_segment_id": "lseg-2770240ef539", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-8b7ed20a5f92", "segment_id": "lseg-68d4d231519f", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "Knowledge of collocations is vital for the competent use of a language: a grammatically correct sentence will stand out as awkward if collocational preferences are violated."}}

segment.text: This makes collocation a common focus for language teaching.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2774-2835", "next_segment_id": "lseg-979aa84cd9a0", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-68d4d231519f", "segment_id": "lseg-2770240ef539", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "This makes collocation a common focus for language teaching."}}

segment.text: Corpus linguists specify a key word in context ( KWIC ) and identify the words immediately surrounding them, to illustrate the way words are used in practice.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2835-2994", "next_segment_id": "lseg-4d7b7d95b60f", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-2770240ef539", "segment_id": "lseg-979aa84cd9a0", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "Corpus linguists specify a key word in context ( KWIC ) and identify the words immediately surrounding them, to illustrate the way words are used in practice."}}

segment.text: The processing of collocations involves a number of parameters, the most important of which is the measure of association , which evaluates whether the co-occurrence is purely by chance or statistically significant .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2994-3211", "next_segment_id": "lseg-6521e8b84282", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-979aa84cd9a0", "segment_id": "lseg-4d7b7d95b60f", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "The processing of collocations involves a number of parameters, the most important of which is the measure of association , which evaluates whether the co-occurrence is purely by chance or statistically significant ."}}

segment.text: Due to the non-random nature of language, most collocations are classed as significant, and the association scores are simply used to rank the results.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3211-3363", "next_segment_id": "lseg-2a99b009153e", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-4d7b7d95b60f", "segment_id": "lseg-6521e8b84282", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "Due to the non-random nature of language, most collocations are classed as significant, and the association scores are simply used to rank the results."}}

segment.text: Commonly used measures of association include mutual information , t scores , and log-likelihood .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3363-3462", "next_segment_id": "lseg-c6663658a9bc", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-6521e8b84282", "segment_id": "lseg-2a99b009153e", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "Commonly used measures of association include mutual information , t scores , and log-likelihood ."}}

segment.text: [ 1 ] [ 2 ] Rather than select a single definition, Gledhill [ 3 ] proposes that collocation involves at least three different perspectives: co-occurrence, a statistical view, which sees collocation as the recurrent appearance in a text of a node and its collocates; [ 4 ] [ 5 ] [ 6 ] construction, which sees collocation either as a correlation between a lexeme and a lexical-grammatical pattern, [ 7 ] or as a relation between a base and its collocative partners; [ 8 ] and expression, a pragmatic view of collocation as a conventional unit of expression, regardless of form.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3462-4040", "next_segment_id": "lseg-2c3d7e760763", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-2a99b009153e", "segment_id": "lseg-c6663658a9bc", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 1 ] [ 2 ] Rather than select a single definition, Gledhill [ 3 ] proposes that collocation involves at least three different perspectives: co-occurrence, a statistical view, which sees collocation as the recurrent appearance in a text of a node and its collocates; [ 4 ] [ 5 ] [ 6 ] construction, which sees collocation either as a correlation between a lexeme and a lexical-grammatical pattern, [ 7 ] or as a relation between a base and its collocative partners; [ 8 ] and expression, a pragmatic view of collocation as a conventional unit of expression, regardless of form."}}

segment.text: [ 9 ] [ 10 ] These different perspectives contrast with the usual way of presenting collocation in phraseological studies.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:4040-4163", "next_segment_id": "lseg-349d8b4f7e11", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-c6663658a9bc", "segment_id": "lseg-2c3d7e760763", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 9 ] [ 10 ] These different perspectives contrast with the usual way of presenting collocation in phraseological studies."}}

segment.text: Traditionally speaking, collocation is explained in terms of all three perspectives at once, in a continuum: Free combination ↔ bound collocation ↔ frozen idiom In dictionaries [ edit ] In 1933, Harold Palmer 's Second Interim Report on English Collocations highlighted the importance of collocation as a key to producing natural-sounding language, for anyone learning a foreign language.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:4163-4552", "next_segment_id": "lseg-00627792f77a", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-2c3d7e760763", "segment_id": "lseg-349d8b4f7e11", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "Traditionally speaking, collocation is explained in terms of all three perspectives at once, in a continuum: Free combination ↔ bound collocation ↔ frozen idiom In dictionaries [ edit ] In 1933, Harold Palmer 's Second Interim Report on English Collocations highlighted the importance of collocation as a key to producing natural-sounding language, for anyone learning a foreign language."}}

segment.text: [ 11 ] Thus from the 1940s onwards, information about recurrent word combinations became a standard feature of monolingual learner's dictionaries .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:4552-4700", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b8da683c6e55", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-349d8b4f7e11", "segment_id": "lseg-00627792f77a", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 11 ] Thus from the 1940s onwards, information about recurrent word combinations became a standard feature of monolingual learner's dictionaries ."}}

segment.text: As these dictionaries became "less word-centred and more phrase-centred", [ 12 ] more attention was paid to collocation.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:4700-4821", "next_segment_id": "lseg-052bfee01ec7", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-00627792f77a", "segment_id": "lseg-b8da683c6e55", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "As these dictionaries became \"less word-centred and more phrase-centred\", [ 12 ] more attention was paid to collocation."}}

segment.text: This trend was supported, from the beginning of the 21st century, by the availability of large text corpora and intelligent corpus-querying software , making it possible to provide a more systematic account of collocation in dictionaries.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:4821-5060", "next_segment_id": "lseg-29cd8d84abf9", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-b8da683c6e55", "segment_id": "lseg-052bfee01ec7", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "This trend was supported, from the beginning of the 21st century, by the availability of large text corpora and intelligent corpus-querying software , making it possible to provide a more systematic account of collocation in dictionaries."}}

segment.text: Using these tools, dictionaries such as the Macmillan English Dictionary and the Longman Dictionary of Contemporary English included boxes or panels with lists of frequent collocations.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:5060-5246", "next_segment_id": "lseg-2f4bcd4a0d4a", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-052bfee01ec7", "segment_id": "lseg-29cd8d84abf9", "source_id": "lsource-b5097878c6b5", "start_time": null, "text": "Using these tools, dictionaries such as the Macmillan English Dictionary and the Longman Dictionary of Contemporary English included boxes or panels with lists of frequent collocations."}}

segment.text: [ 13 ] There are also a number of specialized dictionaries devoted to describing the frequent collocations in a language.

segment.text: [ 15 ] Statistically significant collocation [ edit ] Student's t -test can be used to determine whether the occurrence of a collocation in a corpus is statistically significant.

segment.text: Phrasal verbs ordinarily cannot be understood based upon the meanings of the individual parts alone but must be considered as a whole: the meaning is non- compositional and thus unpredictable.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2573-2766", "next_segment_id": "lseg-21538da2b3be", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-5979111b4ed2", "segment_id": "lseg-52f21811a22c", "source_id": "lsource-eb964e7aff10", "start_time": null, "text": "Phrasal verbs ordinarily cannot be understood based upon the meanings of the individual parts alone but must be considered as a whole: the meaning is non- compositional and thus unpredictable."}}

segment.text: [ a ] Phrasal verbs are differentiated from other classifications of multi-word verbs and free combinations by the criteria of idiomaticity, replacement by a single verb, wh -question formation and particle movement.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2766-2983", "next_segment_id": "lseg-9ef0d7314445", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-52f21811a22c", "segment_id": "lseg-21538da2b3be", "source_id": "lsource-eb964e7aff10", "start_time": null, "text": "[ a ] Phrasal verbs are differentiated from other classifications of multi-word verbs and free combinations by the criteria of idiomaticity, replacement by a single verb, wh -question formation and particle movement."}}

segment.text: [ 1 ] [ 2 ] Terminology [ edit ] In 1900, Frederick Schmidt referred to particle verbs in the Middle English writings of Reginald Pecock as "phrasal verbs" though apparently without intending it as a technical term.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2983-3199", "next_segment_id": "lseg-309115ff1333", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-21538da2b3be", "segment_id": "lseg-9ef0d7314445", "source_id": "lsource-eb964e7aff10", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 1 ] [ 2 ] Terminology [ edit ] In 1900, Frederick Schmidt referred to particle verbs in the Middle English writings of Reginald Pecock as \"phrasal verbs\" though apparently without intending it as a technical term."}}

segment.text: [ 3 ] The term was popularized by Logan Pearsall Smith in Words and Idioms (1925) in which he states that the OED editor Henry Bradley suggested it to him.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3199-3355", "next_segment_id": "lseg-42d5d9bf2d56", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-9ef0d7314445", "segment_id": "lseg-309115ff1333", "source_id": "lsource-eb964e7aff10", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 3 ] The term was popularized by Logan Pearsall Smith in Words and Idioms (1925) in which he states that the OED editor Henry Bradley suggested it to him."}}

segment.text: [ 4 ] This terminology is mainly used in teaching English as a second language .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3355-3436", "next_segment_id": "lseg-549ac938e790", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-309115ff1333", "segment_id": "lseg-42d5d9bf2d56", "source_id": "lsource-eb964e7aff10", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 4 ] This terminology is mainly used in teaching English as a second language ."}}

segment.text: Some textbooks apply the term "phrasal verb" primarily to verbs with particles to distinguish phrasal verbs from verb phrases composed of a verb and a collocated preposition.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3436-3611", "next_segment_id": "lseg-a3f89a818fba", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-42d5d9bf2d56", "segment_id": "lseg-549ac938e790", "source_id": "lsource-eb964e7aff10", "start_time": null, "text": "Some textbooks apply the term \"phrasal verb\" primarily to verbs with particles to distinguish phrasal verbs from verb phrases composed of a verb and a collocated preposition."}}

segment.text: [ 5 ] [ b ] Others include verbs with prepositions under the same category and distinguish particle verbs and prepositional verbs as two types of phrasal verbs.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3611-3772", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b7aab94f6eb6", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-549ac938e790", "segment_id": "lseg-a3f89a818fba", "source_id": "lsource-eb964e7aff10", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 5 ] [ b ] Others include verbs with prepositions under the same category and distinguish particle verbs and prepositional verbs as two types of phrasal verbs."}}

segment.text: [ 6 ] [ c ] Since a prepositional phrase can complement a particle verb, some explanations distinguish three types of phrasal verb constructions depending on whether the verb combines with a particle, a prepositional phrase, or both, [ 7 ] though the third type is not a distinct linguistic phenomenon.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3772-4075", "next_segment_id": "lseg-deb85cb8d16c", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-a3f89a818fba", "segment_id": "lseg-b7aab94f6eb6", "source_id": "lsource-eb964e7aff10", "start_time": null, "text": "[ 6 ] [ c ] Since a prepositional phrase can complement a particle verb, some explanations distinguish three types of phrasal verb constructions depending on whether the verb combines with a particle, a prepositional phrase, or both, [ 7 ] though the third type is not a distinct linguistic phenomenon."}}

segment.text: Finally, some linguists reject the term altogether.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:4075-4127", "next_segment_id": "lseg-8bd9ea195420", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-b7aab94f6eb6", "segment_id": "lseg-deb85cb8d16c", "source_id": "lsource-eb964e7aff10", "start_time": null, "text": "Finally, some linguists reject the term altogether."}}

segment.text: [ d ] Types [ edit ] Verb + particle (particle verbs) [ edit ] Particle verbs (phrasal verbs in the strict sense) are two-word verbs composed of a simple verb and a particle extension that modifies its meaning.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:4127-4338", "next_segment_id": "lseg-cba484c2a047", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-deb85cb8d16c", "segment_id": "lseg-8bd9ea195420", "source_id": "lsource-eb964e7aff10", "start_time": null, "text": "[ d ] Types [ edit ] Verb + particle (particle verbs) [ edit ] Particle verbs (phrasal verbs in the strict sense) are two-word verbs composed of a simple verb and a particle extension that modifies its meaning."}}

segment.text: The particle is thus integrally collocated with the verb.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:4338-4396", "next_segment_id": "lseg-1fcd13d375e5", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-8bd9ea195420", "segment_id": "lseg-cba484c2a047", "source_id": "lsource-eb964e7aff10", "start_time": null, "text": "The particle is thus integrally collocated with the verb."}}

segment.text: In older grammars, the particle was usually analyzed as an adverb.

segment.text: In those examples, the common verbs grow and give are complemented by the particles up and in .

segment.text: The resulting two-word verbs are single semantic units, and so grow up and give in are listed as discrete entries in modern dictionaries.

segment.text: ' - perfect, particle prefixed Similar constructions in non-Germanic languages [ edit ] A number of particle verbs exist in some Romance languages, such as Lombard , spoken in Northern Italy: Fa foeura (to do in: to eat up; to squander); Dà denter (to trade in; to bump into); Borlà giò (to fall down); Lavà sü (to wash up, as in English); Trà sü (to throw up, as in English); Trà vìa (to throw away, as in English); Serà sü (to lock up, as in English); Dà vià (to give away, as in English), and more.

segment.text: In the 2000s, between one and two billion people spoke English, [ 1 ] [ 2 ] making it the largest language by number of speakers , the third largest language by number of native speakers and the most widespread language geographically.

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1700-1936", "next_segment_id": "lseg-0b890340e507", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-5e8d827fda3a", "segment_id": "lseg-328ea5d05d0e", "source_id": "lsource-7b8b21fddf96", "start_time": null, "text": "In the 2000s, between one and two billion people spoke English, [ 1 ] [ 2 ] making it the largest language by number of speakers , the third largest language by number of native speakers and the most widespread language geographically."}}

segment.text: The countries in which English is the native language of most people are sometimes termed the Anglosphere .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:1936-2044", "next_segment_id": "lseg-971da5555491", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-328ea5d05d0e", "segment_id": "lseg-0b890340e507", "source_id": "lsource-7b8b21fddf96", "start_time": null, "text": "The countries in which English is the native language of most people are sometimes termed the Anglosphere ."}}

segment.text: Speakers of English are called Anglophones .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2044-2089", "next_segment_id": "lseg-f782d16f9e74", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-0b890340e507", "segment_id": "lseg-971da5555491", "source_id": "lsource-7b8b21fddf96", "start_time": null, "text": "Speakers of English are called Anglophones ."}}

segment.text: Early Medieval England was the birthplace of the English language; the modern form of the language has been spread around the world since the 17th century, first by the worldwide influence of England and later the United Kingdom , and then by that of the United States .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:2089-2360", "next_segment_id": "lseg-81c6a1b7cdae", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-971da5555491", "segment_id": "lseg-f782d16f9e74", "source_id": "lsource-7b8b21fddf96", "start_time": null, "text": "Early Medieval England was the birthplace of the English language; the modern form of the language has been spread around the world since the 17th century, first by the worldwide influence of England and later the United Kingdom , and then by that of the United States ."}}

segment.text: Through all types of printed and electronic media of these countries, English has become the leading language of international discourse and the lingua franca in many regions and professional fields, such as science , navigation and law .

segment.text: [ 3 ] According to Ethnologue , as of 2025, the United States and India have the most total English speakers, with 319 million and 276 million, respectively.

segment.text: These are followed by Pakistan (112 million), the United Kingdom (65 million), and Nigeria (62 million).

segment.text: Estimates vary, but the general belief is that 35%, 40%, or possibly as many as 45% of the English dictionary have words of French origin.

segment.text: The list, however, only includes words directly borrowed from French, so it includes both joy and joyous but does not include derivatives with English suffixes such as joyful , joyfulness , partisanship , and parenthood .

segment.text: Estimates suggest that at least a third of English vocabulary is of French origin, with some specialists, like scholars, indicating that the proportion may be two-thirds in some registers.

segment.text: Although French is mostly derived from Latin , important other word sources are Gaulish and some Germanic languages , especially Old Frankish .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3761-3905", "next_segment_id": "lseg-7be7da9c572a", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-6712a4c586aa", "segment_id": "lseg-d9dc05e6a31c", "source_id": "lsource-e3c4d32db662", "start_time": null, "text": "Although French is mostly derived from Latin , important other word sources are Gaulish and some Germanic languages , especially Old Frankish ."}}

segment.text: Latin accounts for about 60% of English vocabulary either directly or via a Romance language .

idempotency_key: language.segment.created:{"segment": {"confidence": 1.0, "end_time": null, "locator": "chars:3905-4000", "next_segment_id": "lseg-b07dd5f73c72", "page_locator": "", "previous_segment_id": "lseg-d9dc05e6a31c", "segment_id": "lseg-7be7da9c572a", "source_id": "lsource-e3c4d32db662", "start_time": null, "text": "Latin accounts for about 60% of English vocabulary either directly or via a Romance language ."}}

segment.text: As both English and French have borrowed many words from Latin, determining whether a given Latin word entered English via French or directly from Latin might in some cases be difficult.
